#### Mock exam: C# Foundations Mock Exam

*26 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from the level's bank, from first programs and types to collections, classes, null safety and exceptions.

**Question 1** · One answer · `csharp-basic-01`

What does the C# compiler produce when it builds a program, and how does that become
something the processor can run?

- **✔ A. Intermediate language (IL) in an assembly, which the .NET runtime's just-in-time compiler turns into native code as the program runs**
- B. Native machine code for the current processor, which runs without any .NET runtime installed
- C. Nothing; the runtime reads the `.cs` source files and interprets them line by line every time
- D. JavaScript, which the .NET runtime runs in a built-in browser engine

> **Why:** The compiler translates C# into **intermediate language** (IL, or CIL) and stores it with a
> description of your types (metadata) in an assembly, usually a `.dll`. IL is not tied to a
> processor. When the program runs, the runtime's **JIT compiler** turns each method's IL into
> native code the first time it is called. That is why one assembly runs on both x64 and Arm64
> machines. C# is compiled, not interpreted, and an ordinary build needs the .NET runtime on
> the machine that runs it.

**Question 2** · Select all that apply · `csharp-basic-02`

Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. With top-level statements, the compiler generates the class and the entry-point method that contain them**
- **✔ B. `dotnet run hello.cs` builds and runs a single-file program without a project file**
- C. Every file of a project may contain its own top-level statements
- D. `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>` in the project file turns on warnings about possible null references

> **Why:** Top-level statements are the body of an entry point that the compiler writes for you, so a
> program needs no explicit `class Program` and `static void Main`. Since .NET 10,
> `dotnet run hello.cs` (or `dotnet hello.cs`) runs a **file-based app** with no `.csproj`.
> Only **one** file in a project may contain top-level statements, because a program has one
> entry point. `ImplicitUsings` imports common namespaces such as `System` into every file; the
> null warnings come from a different setting, `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`.

**Question 3** · One answer · `csharp-basic-03`

What happens when this program is compiled and run?

```csharp
var floor = 3;
floor = "third";
Console.WriteLine(floor);
```

- **✔ A. It fails to compile: `floor` is an `int`, and a `string` cannot be assigned to it**
- B. It prints `third`, because `var` lets a variable hold any type
- C. It prints `3`, because the second assignment is ignored
- D. It compiles, then throws an exception at run time when the string is assigned

> **Why:** `var` asks the compiler to infer the type from the initializer. `3` is an `int`, so `floor`
> is an `int` for the rest of its life, exactly as if you had written `int floor = 3;`. The
> second line is error CS0029, "Cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'int'". `var` is not
> a dynamic "any" type, and type errors in C# are found by the compiler, before anything runs.

**Question 4** · One answer · `csharp-basic-04`

What does this line print?

```csharp
Console.WriteLine("Total: " + 2 + 3);
```

- **✔ A. `Total: 23`**
- B. `Total: 5`
- C. `Total: 2 3`
- D. Nothing; it does not compile, because a string and an int cannot be added

> **Why:** `+` is evaluated from left to right. `"Total: " + 2` is a string, `"Total: 2"`, so the next
> `+ 3` appends the character `3` instead of adding numbers. Joining a string with any other
> value is allowed and converts the value to text. To print `Total: 5`, write
> `"Total: " + (2 + 3)` or, more readably, `$"Total: {2 + 3}"`.

**Question 5** · One answer · `csharp-basic-05`

What does this line print?

```csharp
Console.WriteLine($"{17 / 5} {-17 / 5} {-17 % 5} {17 / 5.0}");
```

- **✔ A. `3 -3 -2 3.4`**
- B. `3.4 -3.4 -2 3.4`
- C. `3 -4 3 3.4`
- D. `3 -3 2 3.4`

> **Why:** When both operands are integers, `/` is integer division and rounds **toward zero**: 3 and
> -3, never -4. The remainder `%` takes the sign of the left operand, so `-17 % 5` is -2:
> -3 × 5 is -15, and -17 is 2 below that. Only when one operand is a fractional type, as in `17 / 5.0`, is
> the result 3.4. Answering -4 and 3 is the "round down" rule that some other languages use for
> negative numbers.

**Question 6** · Select all that apply · `csharp-basic-06`

Which of these expressions evaluate to `true`? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `0.1m + 0.2m == 0.3m`**
- B. `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`
- **✔ C. `Math.Round(2.5) == 2`**
- D. `Convert.ToInt32(7.9) == 7`

> **Why:** `decimal` (the `m` suffix) stores decimal digits exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3.
> `double` stores binary fractions, and 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, which is why money
> belongs in `decimal`. `Math.Round` rounds a value exactly halfway to the **even** neighbour
> by default, so 2.5 becomes 2; pass `MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero` to get 3.
> `Convert.ToInt32(7.9)` rounds to the nearest integer, 8. Only a cast, `(int)7.9`, cuts the
> fraction off to give 7.

**Question 7** · One answer · `csharp-basic-07`

What does this program print?

```csharp
bool ok = int.TryParse("4x2", out int n);
Console.WriteLine($"{ok} {n}");
```

- **✔ A. `False 0`**
- B. `True 42`
- C. `False 4`
- D. It throws a `FormatException`

> **Why:** `TryParse` never throws for bad text. It returns `false` and sets the `out` variable to 0.
> It does not skip the letter to make 42, and it does not keep the digits it read before the
> problem. `int.Parse("4x2")` is the method that would throw a `FormatException`. That is why
> `TryParse` is the right choice for anything a person typed.

**Question 8** · One answer · `csharp-basic-08`

What does this program print?

```csharp
string code = " ab ";
code.Trim();
code.ToUpper();
Console.WriteLine($"[{code}]");
```

- **✔ A. `[ ab ]`**
- B. `[AB]`
- C. `[ab]`
- D. `[ AB ]`

> **Why:** Strings are **immutable**. `Trim` and `ToUpper` do not change `code`; each returns a new
> string, and here both results are thrown away. The variable still holds `" ab "`. To keep
> the changes, assign the result: `code = code.Trim().ToUpper();`, which gives `[AB]`. The
> compiler does not warn about the discarded results, so this is an easy bug to miss.

**Question 9** · One answer · `csharp-basic-09`

What does this program print?

```csharp
string[] parts = "red,,blue,".Split(',');
Console.WriteLine(parts.Length);
```

- **✔ A. `4`**
- B. `2`
- C. `3`
- D. `5`

> **Why:** `Split` returns every piece between separators, including empty ones. The pieces are
> `"red"`, `""` (between the two commas), `"blue"` and `""` (after the final comma), so there
> are 4. Answering 2 counts only the non-empty pieces, which is what you get with
> `StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries`. Counting commas plus one, as here, is the reliable
> rule for the default behavior.

**Question 10** · One answer · `csharp-basic-10`

What happens when this program is compiled and run?

```csharp
string day = "Mon";
switch (day)
{
    case "Mon":
        Console.WriteLine("Maintenance");
    case "Tue":
        Console.WriteLine("Open");
        break;
}
```

- **✔ A. It fails to compile, because the `"Mon"` section does not end with `break`**
- B. It prints `Maintenance` and then `Open`, falling through as in C
- C. It prints only `Maintenance`, because a missing `break` is added automatically
- D. It compiles with a warning and prints `Maintenance`

> **Why:** C# never lets one `switch` section fall through into the next. Every section that contains
> statements must end with `break`, `return`, `throw` or `goto`, so the compiler reports error
> CS0163, "Control cannot fall through from one case label ('case "Mon":') to another". This
> rule removes a classic C bug. To share code between values, stack the labels instead:
> `case "Sat": case "Sun":` followed by one section.

**Question 11** · One answer · `csharp-basic-11`

What does this program print?

```csharp
int calls = 0;
bool a = Check(false) && Check(true);
bool b = Check(true) || Check(false);
Console.WriteLine($"{a} {b} {calls}");

bool Check(bool result)
{
    calls++;
    return result;
}
```

- **✔ A. `False True 2`**
- B. `False True 4`
- C. `True True 2`
- D. `False False 4`

> **Why:** `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: they evaluate the right-hand side only when it can change
> the result. `false && anything` is already `false`, so the second `Check` is not called.
> `true || anything` is already `true`, so again only one call happens. That makes two calls
> in total. Short-circuiting is what makes `s != null && s.Length > 0` safe. The operators `&`
> and `|` evaluate both sides and would give 4.

**Question 12** · One answer · `csharp-basic-12`

What does this program print?

```csharp
int n = 10;
int steps = 0;
do
{
    n -= 4;
    steps++;
} while (n > 0);
Console.WriteLine($"{n} {steps}");
```

- **✔ A. `-2 3`**
- B. `2 2`
- C. `-2 2`
- D. `6 1`

> **Why:** Trace it: 10 becomes 6 (step 1), then 2 (step 2), then -2 (step 3). The condition is checked
> **after** each run of the body, so the loop stops only once `n > 0` is false, which is when
> `n` is -2. Answering `2 2` stops one iteration early, as if the condition were checked before
> subtracting. A `do` loop always runs its body at least once; a `while` loop checks first.

**Question 13** · One answer · `csharp-basic-13`

What does this program print?

```csharp
int a = 5;
int b = 5;
AddOne(a);
AddOneRef(ref b);
Console.WriteLine($"{a} {b}");

static void AddOne(int x) => x++;
static void AddOneRef(ref int x) => x++;
```

- **✔ A. `5 6`**
- B. `6 6`
- C. `5 5`
- D. Nothing: `ref` can only be used with reference types

> **Why:** By default an argument is **passed by value**: `AddOne` receives a copy of `a` and increments
> the copy, so `a` stays 5. `ref` passes the variable itself, so `AddOneRef` changes `b` to 6.
> `ref` works with any type, and it must be written both in the method's parameter list and at
> the call, as in `AddOneRef(ref b)`. In everyday code, returning the new value is usually
> clearer than `ref`.

**Question 14** · Select all that apply · `csharp-basic-14`

Given this method, which calls compile? Select all that apply.

```csharp
static class Shop
{
    public static decimal Cost(decimal weight, int boxes = 1, bool express = false) =>
        (weight + boxes) * (express ? 2 : 1);
}
```

- **✔ A. `Shop.Cost(2m, express: true)`**
- **✔ B. `Shop.Cost(express: true, weight: 2m)`**
- C. `Shop.Cost(2m, , true)`
- D. `Shop.Cost(boxes: 2)`

> **Why:** `boxes` and `express` are optional because they have default values. A **named argument**
> skips straight to a parameter, so `Cost(2m, express: true)` leaves `boxes` at 1, and named
> arguments may come in any order when all of them are named. C# has no syntax for an empty
> gap: `Cost(2m, , true)` is error CS0839, "Argument missing". `weight` has no default, so
> leaving it out is error CS7036, which names the missing required parameter.

**Question 15** · One answer · `csharp-basic-15`

What happens when this program runs?

```csharp
List<string> names = ["Ama", "", "Bo"];
foreach (string name in names)
{
    if (name == "")
    {
        names.Remove(name);
    }
}
Console.WriteLine(names.Count);
```

- **✔ A. It throws an `InvalidOperationException`, because the list changed during the `foreach` loop**
- B. It prints `2`
- C. It prints `3`, because `Remove` inside a loop is ignored
- D. It fails to compile, because the loop variable is read-only

> **Why:** A `foreach` loop over a `List<T>` checks on every step that the list has not changed. After
> `Remove`, the next step throws `InvalidOperationException`: "Collection was modified;
> enumeration operation may not execute." The loop variable is read-only, but calling a
> method on the list is allowed, so it compiles. To remove while looping, walk the indexes
> backwards with `for` and `RemoveAt`, or use `names.RemoveAll(...)` after the loop.

**Question 16** · One answer · `csharp-basic-16`

What does this program print?

```csharp
int[] a = [1, 2, 3];
int[] b = a;
b[0] = 9;
List<int> c = new List<int>(a);
c[1] = 8;
Console.WriteLine($"{a[0]} {a[1]}");
```

- **✔ A. `9 2`**
- B. `1 2`
- C. `9 8`
- D. `1 8`

> **Why:** Arrays are reference types. `int[] b = a;` copies the **reference**, so `a` and `b` are two
> names for one array, and writing through `b` changes what `a` sees: 9. `new List<int>(a)`
> creates a **new** list with copies of the elements, so changing `c[1]` leaves the array
> alone: 2. Assignment shares; constructing a new collection copies.

**Question 17** · One answer · `csharp-basic-17`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var stock = new Dictionary<string, int>();
stock["bolt"] = 5;
stock["nut"] = 2;
stock["bolt"] = 8;
stock["nut"] += 1;
Console.WriteLine($"{stock.Count} {stock["bolt"]} {stock["nut"]} {stock.GetValueOrDefault("gear")}");
```

- **✔ A. `2 8 3 0`**
- B. `3 13 3 0`
- C. `2 13 3 0`
- D. It throws `KeyNotFoundException` for `"gear"`

> **Why:** Assigning through the indexer **adds** a missing key and **replaces** the value of an
> existing one, so `bolt` is 8 (not 13) and there are still two keys. `stock["nut"] += 1`
> reads 2 and stores 3. Reading a missing key with the indexer would throw
> `KeyNotFoundException`, but `GetValueOrDefault` returns the default, 0, instead. Only
> `Add("bolt", 8)` would have thrown, because `Add` refuses duplicate keys.

**Question 18** · Select all that apply · `csharp-basic-18`

Which statements about `HashSet<T>` are true? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `Add` returns `false` when the value is already in the set, and the set is unchanged**
- B. A `HashSet<T>` returns its values in the order they were added
- **✔ C. `Contains` stays fast as the set grows, unlike `Contains` on a `List<T>`, which checks the elements one by one**
- D. `IntersectWith` returns a new set and leaves the original unchanged

> **Why:** A set holds each value once, and `Add` tells you whether the value was new, which makes "have
> I seen this?" a single call. Sets are built for fast lookups, while `List<T>.Contains`
> compares with every element in turn. A set promises **no** order: sort its values if order
> matters. `IntersectWith`, `UnionWith` and `ExceptWith` change the set they are called on and
> return nothing, so copy the set first, with `new HashSet<T>(original)`, to keep the original.

**Question 19** · One answer · `csharp-basic-19`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var a = new Box { Size = 1 };
var b = a;
b.Size = 2;
var c = new Box { Size = 2 };
Console.WriteLine($"{a.Size} {a == b} {a == c}");

class Box
{
    public int Size { get; set; }
}
```

- **✔ A. `2 True False`**
- B. `1 False False`
- C. `2 True True`
- D. `1 True True`

> **Why:** A class is a reference type. `var b = a;` copies the reference, so there is one `Box` with
> two names, and setting `b.Size` changes what `a.Size` shows: 2. For classes, `==` compares
> **references** by default: `a == b` is `true` because they are the same object, and
> `a == c` is `false` because `c` is a different object, even though its `Size` is equal.

**Question 20** · One answer · `csharp-basic-20`

This program does not compile. Why?

```csharp
var badge = new Badge("Ines");
badge.Name = "Omar";

class Badge
{
    public Badge(string name) => Name = name;

    public string Name { get; }
}
```

- **✔ A. `Name` has only a `get` accessor, so it can be set in the constructor but nowhere else**
- B. `Name` is private, because properties are private unless declared `public`
- C. A constructor cannot be written with `=>`
- D. `badge` was declared with `var`, so its properties cannot be assigned

> **Why:** `{ get; }` makes a **read-only** auto-implemented property: the constructor may set it, and
> every other assignment is error CS0200, "Property or indexer 'Badge.Name' cannot be assigned
> to". The property is `public`, so reading it from outside is fine. Expression-bodied
> constructors are allowed, and `var` has nothing to do with it. To allow changes, use
> `{ get; set; }`; to allow setting only in an object initializer, use `{ get; init; }`.

**Question 21** · One answer · `csharp-basic-21`

What does this program print?

```csharp
string? name = null;
int? length = name?.Length;
Console.WriteLine(length ?? -1);
name ??= "Ada";
Console.WriteLine(name.Length);
```

- **✔ A. `-1`, then `3`**
- B. It throws a `NullReferenceException` on the second line
- C. `0`, then `3`
- D. Nothing: it does not compile, because `name` may be `null` on the last line

> **Why:** `name?.Length` gives `null` instead of throwing when `name` is `null`, which is why its type
> is `int?`. `?? -1` replaces that `null` with -1. `??=` assigns `"Ada"` only because `name` is
> `null`, and after it the compiler's null-state analysis knows `name` is not `null`, so the
> last line compiles without even a warning and prints 3. A missing value never silently
> becomes 0.

**Question 22** · True or false · `csharp-basic-22`

True or false: writing the null-forgiving operator, as in `name!.Length`, makes the compiler
insert a check, so the line can no longer throw a `NullReferenceException`.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** `!` only tells the compiler "trust me, this is not null" and silences its warning. It
> generates no check: if `name` is `null` at run time, `name!.Length` still throws
> `NullReferenceException`, and now without any warning that it might. Nullable annotations
> and `!` exist only at compile time. Prefer a real check (`is not null`), a default with
> `??`, or a non-nullable type.

**Question 23** · One answer · `csharp-basic-23`

What does this program print?

```csharp
try
{
    Console.Write("A ");
    int.Parse("x");
    Console.Write("B ");
}
catch (FormatException)
{
    Console.Write("C ");
}
finally
{
    Console.Write("D ");
}
Console.WriteLine("E");
```

- **✔ A. `A C D E`**
- B. `A B C D E`
- C. `A C E`
- D. `A C D` and then the program stops

> **Why:** `int.Parse("x")` throws a `FormatException`, so the rest of the `try` block, including
> `B`, is skipped. The matching `catch` runs (`C`), then the `finally` block, which always runs
> when control leaves the `try` (`D`). Because the exception was handled, the program then
> continues after the whole statement and prints `E`.

**Question 24** · Select all that apply · `csharp-basic-24`

A method throws `new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(day), "Too early.")`. Which `catch`
clauses, placed around the call, catch it? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `catch (ArgumentOutOfRangeException)`**
- **✔ B. `catch (ArgumentException)`**
- **✔ C. `catch (Exception)`**
- D. `catch (InvalidOperationException)`

> **Why:** A `catch` clause handles its exception type **and every type derived from it**.
> `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` derives from `ArgumentException`, which derives from
> `Exception`, so all three of those clauses match. `InvalidOperationException` is a separate
> branch of the family and does not. This is also why specific clauses must come first: a
> `catch (Exception)` placed first would catch everything, and the compiler rejects any clause
> after it with error CS0160.

**Question 25** · One answer · `csharp-basic-25`

What does this program print?

```csharp
List<string> lines = ["# note", "3", "", "x", "5"];
List<int> bad = [];
for (int i = 0; i < lines.Count; i++)
{
    string line = lines[i].Trim();
    if (line.Length == 0 || line.StartsWith('#'))
    {
        continue;
    }
    if (!int.TryParse(line, out int value))
    {
        bad.Add(i + 1);
    }
}
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", bad));
```

- **✔ A. `4`**
- B. `3`
- C. `2`
- D. `1`

> **Why:** The loop numbers **every** line, including the note and the blank line it skips, so the
> numbers match what a person sees in an editor. `"x"` is at index 3, and `i + 1` reports line
> 4. Answering 3 forgets the `+ 1`; answering 2 numbers only the lines that were not skipped.
> Number first, then decide what to skip.

**Question 26** · True or false · `csharp-basic-26`

True or false: when standard input has ended, `Console.ReadLine()` returns an empty string,
`""`.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** It returns `null`, which is why its return type is `string?`. An empty string means the user
> entered an empty line, which is ordinary input and should usually be skipped, not treated as
> the end. A loop that reads all input therefore stops on `line is null`. Calling a method such
> as `Trim()` on the result without checking gives warning CS8602 and a
> `NullReferenceException` at the end of the input.

#### Lab: Tool Library Lending Desk

*C# · about 50 minutes · 5 s per test.* Track which member has which tool, charge late fees to the day, and replay the desk's text log without ever crashing on a bad line.

**Scenario**

The Maplewood Tool Library lends drills, saws, ladders and sanders to its members, so that a
street needs one ladder instead of forty. Volunteers run the lending desk on weekends and type
every transaction into a plain text log:

```text
# Saturday desk, volunteer: Priya
1 OUT drill-04 m1032
2 OUT LADDER-2 M2001
9 IN DRILL-04
```

A line says on which day of the season something happened, whether a tool went `OUT` to a member
or came back `IN`, and which tool and member it was. A loan lasts a fixed number of days. Every
day a tool is kept beyond that costs a small late fee, and a member may hold at most three tools.

Until now a spreadsheet macro read the log. It treated `drill-04` and `DRILL-04` as two
different drills, charged a day too much whenever a tool came back exactly on time, and stopped
with an error on the first line a tired volunteer had mistyped, so nothing after it was counted.

You are writing its replacement: a small C# library that knows the rules, and a replay method
that applies a whole log, skips what it should, and reports exactly which lines it could not
apply, so a volunteer can fix them, without ever crashing.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.cs`. The starter declares every type and member the tests use. Keep their names,
parameters and return types. You may add private fields and private methods. Do not add
top-level statements or a `Main` method.

**Ids.** A tool id or member id is compared after removing the spaces around it and converting
it to upper case, so `" drill-04"` and `"DRILL-04"` are the same tool. Every method that takes an
id stores and returns ids in this normalized form.

1. `public static string NormalizeId(string id)` returns `id.Trim().ToUpperInvariant()`. If `id`
   is empty or contains only whitespace, it throws `ArgumentException`. Every method below that
   takes an id calls it, so a blank id makes any of them throw `ArgumentException`.
2. `public ToolLibrary(int loanDays, decimal lateFeePerDay)` throws
   `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when `loanDays` is less than 1 or `lateFeePerDay` is negative.
   Otherwise it sets the properties `LoanDays` and `LateFeePerDay`. A fee of `0` is allowed.
3. `public void Lend(string toolId, string memberId, int day)` lends a tool. Check in this order
   and throw at the first problem:
   - a blank tool id or member id: `ArgumentException`;
   - `day` below 0: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`;
   - the tool is already on loan, to anyone: `InvalidOperationException`;
   - the member already holds `MaxToolsPerMember` (3) tools: `InvalidOperationException`.

   Otherwise record the loan. A method that throws must not change anything.
4. `public decimal Return(string toolId, int day)` takes a tool back and returns the late fee
   charged for it. Check in this order:
   - a blank tool id: `ArgumentException`;
   - the tool is not on loan: `InvalidOperationException`;
   - `day` is earlier than the day the tool was lent: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

   The tool was kept for `day - dayLent` days. Each day beyond `LoanDays` costs
   `LateFeePerDay`, so a tool returned after exactly `LoanDays` days costs nothing. Remove the
   loan, add the fee to what the member owes, and return the fee (`0` when it was on time).
5. `public string? HolderOf(string toolId)` returns the normalized id of the member who has the
   tool, or `null` when it is not on loan.
6. `public List<string> ToolsHeldBy(string memberId)` returns the normalized ids of the member's
   tools, sorted with `StringComparer.Ordinal`, or an empty list.
7. `public decimal FeesOwedBy(string memberId)` returns the total of every fee charged to the
   member so far, or `0`.
8. `public string Describe(string memberId)` returns one line in exactly this form, using the
   singular `tool` only for exactly one tool and the fees with two decimals and a dot
   (`ToString("F2", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`):

   ```text
   M1032: 1 tool out, owes 0.50
   M2001: 0 tools out, owes 1.50
   ```
9. `public static List<int> DeskLog.Replay(ToolLibrary library, string text)` applies a whole
   log to `library` and returns the numbers of the lines it could not apply, in increasing
   order.
   - Lines end with `\n` or `\r\n`. They are numbered from 1, and every line counts, including
     the ones that are skipped.
   - Skip a line that is empty or only whitespace, and a line whose first non-whitespace
     character is `#`.
   - Fields are separated by one or more spaces, and spaces at either end of a line are
     ignored. A line is `DAY OUT TOOL MEMBER` (four fields) or `DAY IN TOOL` (three fields).
   - Reject the line when `DAY` is not a whole number of 0 or more, when the action is not
     exactly `OUT` or `IN` (in capitals), or when the number of fields does not match the
     action.
   - Otherwise call `Lend` or `Return`. If that throws `ArgumentException` (which includes
     `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`) or `InvalidOperationException`, reject the line.
   - Carry on with the next line after a rejected one. `Replay` never throws, whatever the text.

Example, the start of a Saturday shift with a loan period of 7 days and a fee of 0.50 a day:

```csharp
var library = new ToolLibrary(7, 0.50m);
string log =
    "# Saturday desk, volunteer: Priya\n" +   // line 1: skipped
    "1 OUT drill-04 m1032\n" +                // line 2
    "1 OUT SAW-11 M1032\n" +                  // line 3
    "2 OUT LADDER-2 M2001\n" +                // line 4
    "3 OUT DRILL-04 M2001\n" +                // line 5: rejected, DRILL-04 is already out
    "\n" +                                    // line 6: skipped
    "9 IN DRILL-04\n" +                       // line 7: kept 8 days, 1 day late, fee 0.50
    "10 BORROW SAW-11 M1032\n" +              // line 8: rejected, unknown action
    "12 IN ladder-2\n";                       // line 9: kept 10 days, 3 days late, fee 1.50

List<int> rejected = DeskLog.Replay(library, log);   // [5, 8]
library.HolderOf("saw-11");                          // "M1032"
library.HolderOf("DRILL-04");                        // null
library.Describe("M1032");                           // "M1032: 1 tool out, owes 0.50"
library.Describe("m2001");                           // "M2001: 0 tools out, owes 1.50"
```

**Tips.** Write `NormalizeId` first and use it everywhere. Decide whether to skip a line before
you split it: a comment may contain anything. Test your `Return` with a tool that comes back
exactly on time.

**Test cases the backend runs**

**Test 1: Replays the Saturday shift from the instructions** (visible)

```csharp
// The Saturday shift from the instructions, replayed line by line.
var library = new ToolLibrary(7, 0.50m);
string log =
    "# Saturday desk, volunteer: Priya\n" +
    "1 OUT drill-04 m1032\n" +
    "1 OUT SAW-11 M1032\n" +
    "2 OUT LADDER-2 M2001\n" +
    "3 OUT DRILL-04 M2001\n" +
    "\n" +
    "9 IN DRILL-04\n" +
    "10 BORROW SAW-11 M1032\n" +
    "12 IN ladder-2\n";

List<int> rejected = DeskLog.Replay(library, log);

Check.SequenceEqual(rejected, new[] { 5, 8 },
    "Replay returns the numbers of the lines it could not apply, counting comment and blank lines");
Check.Equal(library.OnLoanCount, 1, "OnLoanCount after the shift");
Check.Equal(library.HolderOf("saw-11"), "M1032", "HolderOf finds the member who has SAW-11, whatever the case of the id");
Check.Equal(library.HolderOf("DRILL-04"), null, "HolderOf is null for a tool that came back");
Check.Equal(library.FeesOwedBy("M1032"), 0.50m, "FeesOwedBy for the member who kept DRILL-04 one day too long");
Check.Equal(library.Describe("m2001"), "M2001: 0 tools out, owes 1.50", "Describe for the member who returned LADDER-2 late");
Check.Equal(library.Describe("M1032"), "M1032: 1 tool out, owes 0.50", "Describe for the member who still has SAW-11");
```

**Test 2: Enforces the rules for ids, lending and returning** (hidden)

```csharp
// Ids, the constructor, Lend and Return follow the rules in the instructions.
Check.True(ToolLibrary.NormalizeId("  drill-04 ") == "DRILL-04",
    "NormalizeId trims the id and converts it to upper case");
Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => ToolLibrary.NormalizeId(""), "NormalizeId rejects an empty id");
Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => ToolLibrary.NormalizeId("   "), "NormalizeId rejects an id made of spaces");

Check.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => new ToolLibrary(0, 1m), "the constructor rejects a loan period below one day");
Check.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => new ToolLibrary(7, -0.01m), "the constructor rejects a negative late fee");
var free = new ToolLibrary(1, 0m);
Check.True(free.LoanDays == 1 && free.LateFeePerDay == 0m && free.OnLoanCount == 0,
    "a one-day loan period and a fee of zero are allowed, and are reported by the properties");

var library = new ToolLibrary(7, 0.50m);
Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => library.Lend("DRILL-04", " ", 1), "Lend rejects a blank member id");
Check.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => library.Lend("", "M1", 1), "Lend rejects a blank tool id");
Check.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => library.Lend("DRILL-04", "M1", -1), "Lend rejects a negative day");
Check.True(library.OnLoanCount == 0, "a rejected Lend changes nothing");

library.Lend("drill-04", "m1", 0);
Check.True(library.HolderOf("DRILL-04") == "M1", "Lend stores both ids in their normalized form, and day 0 is allowed");
Check.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => library.Lend(" Drill-04", "M2", 2),
    "Lend refuses a tool that is already on loan, even when the id is written differently");
Check.True(library.HolderOf("drill-04") == "M1", "a refused Lend leaves the earlier loan in place");

library.Lend("SAW-11", "M1", 1);
library.Lend("ladder-2", "M1", 1);
Check.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => library.Lend("SANDER-3", "m1", 2),
    "Lend refuses a fourth tool for the same member");
Check.True(library.HolderOf("SANDER-3") is null && library.OnLoanCount == 3, "a refused fourth loan is not recorded");
Check.True(string.Join(",", library.ToolsHeldBy(" m1")) == "DRILL-04,LADDER-2,SAW-11",
    "ToolsHeldBy lists a member's tools as normalized ids in ordinal order");
Check.True(library.ToolsHeldBy("M9").Count == 0, "ToolsHeldBy is an empty list for a member with no tools");

Check.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => library.Return("SANDER-3", 5), "Return refuses a tool that is not on loan");
Check.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => library.Return("SAW-11", 0),
    "Return refuses a day before the day the tool was lent");
Check.True(library.HolderOf("SAW-11") == "M1", "a refused Return leaves the tool on loan");

library.Return("saw-11", 3);
Check.True(library.HolderOf("SAW-11") is null && library.OnLoanCount == 2, "Return takes the tool off loan");
library.Lend("SANDER-3", "M1", 3);
Check.True(library.HolderOf("sander-3") == "M1", "after a return the member may borrow a third tool again");
Check.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => library.Return("SAW-11", 4), "a tool cannot be returned twice");
```

**Test 3: Charges late fees to the day and describes members exactly** (hidden)

```csharp
// Late fees are exact to the day, add up per member, and Describe formats them.
var library = new ToolLibrary(7, 0.25m);

library.Lend("A1", "M7", 10);
Check.True(library.Return("A1", 10) == 0m, "a tool returned on the day it was lent costs nothing");
library.Lend("A1", "M7", 10);
Check.True(library.Return("A1", 17) == 0m, "a tool kept exactly the loan period costs nothing");
library.Lend("A1", "M7", 10);
Check.True(library.Return("A1", 18) == 0.25m, "one day over the loan period costs one day's fee");
library.Lend("A1", "M7", 10);
Check.True(library.Return("A1", 20) == 0.75m, "three days over the loan period cost three days' fees");
Check.True(library.FeesOwedBy("m7") == 1.00m, "FeesOwedBy adds up every fee the member was charged");
Check.True(library.FeesOwedBy("M8") == 0m, "FeesOwedBy is zero for a member who was never charged");

Check.True(library.Describe(" m7 ") == "M7: 0 tools out, owes 1.00",
    "Describe uses the normalized id, the plural for zero tools and two decimals");
library.Lend("B2", "M7", 30);
Check.True(library.Describe("M7") == "M7: 1 tool out, owes 1.00", "Describe uses the singular for exactly one tool");
library.Lend("C3", "M7", 30);
Check.True(library.Describe("M7") == "M7: 2 tools out, owes 1.00", "Describe uses the plural for two tools");
Check.True(library.Describe("M8") == "M8: 0 tools out, owes 0.00", "Describe works for a member the library has never seen");

var daily = new ToolLibrary(1, 1.10m);
daily.Lend("D4", "M3", 5);
daily.Lend("E5", "M3", 5);
Check.True(daily.Return("D4", 9) == 3.30m, "the fee is the number of late days times the fee per day");
daily.Return("E5", 20);
Check.True(daily.FeesOwedBy("M3") == 18.70m, "fees from several returns add up for the member");
Check.True(daily.Describe("m3") == "M3: 0 tools out, owes 18.70", "Describe shows a total with two decimals");

var gift = new ToolLibrary(3, 0m);
gift.Lend("F6", "M4", 0);
Check.True(gift.Return("F6", 100) == 0m && gift.FeesOwedBy("M4") == 0m, "with a fee of zero nobody is charged");
```

**Test 4: Replays messy logs, line endings and refused lines without crashing** (hidden)

```csharp
// Replay skips what it should, rejects what it cannot read or apply, and never throws.
var empty = new ToolLibrary(7, 1m);
Check.True(DeskLog.Replay(empty, "").Count == 0, "an empty log rejects nothing");
Check.True(DeskLog.Replay(empty, "# closed today\n\n   \n  # 1 OUT A1 M1\n").Count == 0 && empty.OnLoanCount == 0,
    "comment lines, including indented ones that look like entries, and blank lines are skipped");

var library = new ToolLibrary(7, 1m);
string windowsLog = "1 OUT A1 M1\r\n2 OUT B2 M2\r\n\r\n4 IN A1\r\n";
Check.True(DeskLog.Replay(library, windowsLog).Count == 0, "lines that end with \\r\\n are read like lines that end with \\n");
Check.True(library.HolderOf("A1") is null && library.HolderOf("B2") == "M2", "every line of a \\r\\n log is applied");

var unreadable = new ToolLibrary(7, 1m);
string badLines =
    "-1 OUT A1 M1\n" +
    "two OUT A1 M1\n" +
    "3.5 OUT A1 M1\n" +
    "4 out A1 M1\n" +
    "4 OUT A1\n" +
    "4 IN A1 M1\n" +
    "4\n" +
    "4 IN\n" +
    "4 LEND A1 M1\n";
List<int> rejected = DeskLog.Replay(unreadable, badLines);
Check.True(rejected.Count == 9, "a bad day, a lower-case or unknown action and a wrong number of fields each reject the line");
Check.True(unreadable.OnLoanCount == 0, "a rejected line changes nothing");

var spaced = new ToolLibrary(7, 1m);
Check.True(DeskLog.Replay(spaced, "  5   OUT   a1    m1  \n").Count == 0 && spaced.HolderOf("A1") == "M1",
    "fields may be separated by several spaces and surrounded by spaces");

var busy = new ToolLibrary(2, 0.50m);
string busyLog =
    "1 OUT A1 M1\n" +
    "1 OUT A2 M1\n" +
    "# M1 reaches the limit of three tools on the next line\n" +
    "1 OUT A3 M1\n" +
    "2 OUT A4 m1\n" +
    "2 IN Z9\n" +
    "0 IN A1\n" +
    "6 IN A1\n" +
    "7 OUT A4 M1\n" +
    "8 OUT A1 M2\n";
List<int> refused = DeskLog.Replay(busy, busyLog);
Check.True(string.Join(",", refused) == "5,6,7",
    "lines the library refuses are rejected, and the lines after them are still applied");
Check.True(busy.HolderOf("A4") == "M1" && busy.HolderOf("A1") == "M2" && busy.FeesOwedBy("M1") == 1.50m,
    "the state after a log with refused lines matches applying only the accepted lines");

var noisy = new ToolLibrary(7, 1m);
string garbage = "\u0000\n,,,,\nOUT OUT OUT OUT\n99999999999 OUT A1 M1\n1 IN\t\n1 OUT \t A1 M1\n#\n";
bool threw = false;
try
{
    DeskLog.Replay(noisy, garbage);
}
catch (Exception)
{
    threw = true;
}
Check.True(!threw, "Replay never throws, whatever the log contains");
```

### Level II · Medium: Types, Generics and LINQ

The C# type system in depth: structs, enums, tuples and records, value and reference semantics, inheritance, interfaces and encapsulation, then generics, the collection interfaces, delegates and lambdas, LINQ, pattern matching and the extension members of C# 14. The level ends with a lab that builds a small library-loans service from all of them.

**After this level you can**

- Design value types, classes, records and enums that fit their data, and predict how copying and equality behave for each
- Build class hierarchies with virtual, abstract and sealed members, and describe capabilities with interfaces such as IComparable and IEquatable
- Encapsulate state with access modifiers and properties, including the C# 14 field keyword, and write generic types and methods with constraints
- Process data with delegates, lambdas and LINQ queries, choosing the right collection and avoiding the traps of deferred execution
- Express decisions with pattern matching and switch expressions, and extend existing types with extension methods and C# 14 extension members

#### Lesson 1: Structs, Enums and Tuples

*25 minutes.* Define your own value types with `struct`, name a fixed set of choices with `enum` (including combinable flags), and group values on the fly with tuples and deconstruction.

**Objectives**

- Define a `readonly struct` with a constructor, a computed property and a `Deconstruct` method, and predict its default value
- Convert an enum to and from its number and its name, and validate a number that came from outside
- Build a `[Flags]` enum and add, remove and test flags with `|`, `&` and `~`
- Return several values from a method as a named tuple and deconstruct the result, using discards where needed

**Outline**

1. Value types you define yourself
2. Defining a struct
3. Enums
4. Flags: several choices at once
5. Tuples and deconstruction

#### Lesson 2: Value and Reference Semantics

*30 minutes.* Predict what assignment, comparison and method calls do to value types and reference types, write equality that hash-based collections can rely on, and recognise boxing.

**Objectives**

- Predict the result of copying and then changing a struct and a class
- Choose between `==`, `Equals` and `ReferenceEquals`, and override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` together
- Explain boxing and unboxing and spot the code that causes them
- Explain what `ref` and `in` change for a value-type parameter and for a reference-type parameter

**Outline**

1. Where the data lives
2. Copying
3. Equality: `==`, `Equals` and `ReferenceEquals`
4. `GetHashCode` must agree with `Equals`
5. Boxing
6. What `ref` and `in` change

#### Lesson 3: Inheritance and Polymorphism

*30 minutes.* Build a class hierarchy in which derived classes reuse and replace the behaviour of a base class, and call the right version of a method through a base-class variable.

**Objectives**

- Derive a class from a base class and chain its constructor to the base constructor with `base(...)`
- Make a member replaceable with `virtual` or required with `abstract`, and replace it with `override`
- Predict which method runs when a call goes through a base-class variable, with `override` and with `new`
- Use `protected` and `sealed` to control what derived classes can see and do

**Outline**

1. Base and derived classes
2. Constructors and `base`
3. `virtual`, `override` and polymorphism
4. `abstract` and `sealed`
5. Hiding with `new`, and casting

#### Lesson 4: Interfaces

*30 minutes.* Describe a capability as an interface, implement it in unrelated classes and structs, and use the standard interfaces that let .NET sort and compare your types.

**Objectives**

- Define an interface and implement it in several types, including more than one interface per type
- Write methods and collections that depend on an interface instead of a concrete class
- Use a default interface method and an explicit implementation, and say through which variables each can be called
- Implement `IComparable<T>` and `IEquatable<T>` so that `Sort`, `Contains` and hash-based collections work

**Outline**

1. An interface is a contract
2. Programming against the interface
3. Default interface methods
4. Explicit implementation
5. `IComparable<T>` and `IEquatable<T>`

#### Lesson 5: Records and Immutability

*30 minutes.* Build data types whose values cannot change after creation, with `init` and `required` properties and with records, and make modified copies with `with` expressions.

**Objectives**

- Use `init` and `required` so that an object is fully set up at creation and cannot be changed afterwards
- Declare positional record classes and record structs, and list the members the compiler generates for them
- Create modified copies with a `with` expression and predict the result of comparing records
- Explain why record immutability is shallow and what that means for collection properties

**Outline**

1. Why immutable data
2. `init` accessors
3. `required` members
4. Records
5. `with` expressions
6. Record structs
7. Immutability is shallow

#### Lesson 6: Properties and Encapsulation

*25 minutes.* Protect an object's data behind access modifiers and properties, validate values with the C# 14 `field` keyword, add indexers, and assign through possibly null references with `?.`.

**Objectives**

- Choose the narrowest access modifier for a type or member from the six C# offers
- Write auto-properties with restricted setters, computed properties and validating setters that use `field`
- Declare an indexer so that an object can be used with square brackets
- Use null-conditional assignment and say when its right-hand side is evaluated

**Outline**

1. Encapsulation
2. Access modifiers
3. Restricted setters and computed properties
4. Validation with `field`
5. Indexers
6. Null-conditional assignment

#### Lesson 7: Generics

*30 minutes.* Write one method or class that works for many types without giving up type safety, constrain its type parameters to the operations it needs, and see why generics beat `object`.

**Objectives**

- Explain the type-safety and boxing problems of storing values as `object`, and how generics remove them
- Write generic methods and let the compiler infer their type arguments
- Constrain a type parameter with an interface, a base class, `new()`, `class`, `struct` or `notnull`, and read error CS0311
- Write a generic class that uses `default` for a type parameter

**Outline**

1. The problem with `object`
2. Generic methods
3. Constraints
4. Generic classes and `default`
5. How generics run

#### Lesson 8: Collections and Their Interfaces

*30 minutes.* Learn the interfaces every .NET collection implements, use them to accept and return collections safely, and add queues, stacks and sorted collections to your toolkit.

**Objectives**

- Describe what `IEnumerable<T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `IList<T>` and the read-only interfaces each add
- Choose parameter and return types so that methods accept any suitable collection and callers cannot corrupt internal state
- Use `Queue<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue>` and `SortedSet<T>` for the jobs they fit
- Pick a collection for a task from its access pattern and the cost of its operations

**Outline**

1. One family of interfaces
2. Accept little, return safely
3. `Queue<T>` and `Stack<T>`
4. Sorted collections
5. Choosing a collection

#### Lesson 9: Delegates and Lambdas

*30 minutes.* Treat behaviour as a value, store methods in delegates, write lambdas for `Func`, `Action` and `Predicate`, and predict what a lambda sees when it captures a variable.

**Objectives**

- Declare a delegate type, assign methods to it and invoke it
- Choose between `Func`, `Action` and `Predicate` and write expression and statement lambdas for them
- Pass behaviour into a method as a delegate parameter
- Predict the output of code whose lambdas capture outer variables, including inside `for` and `foreach` loops

**Outline**

1. A delegate is a type for methods
2. `Func`, `Action` and `Predicate`
3. Lambda expressions
4. Closures: lambdas that capture variables
5. `static` lambdas and combined delegates

#### Lesson 10: LINQ Fundamentals

*30 minutes.* Query in-memory data with LINQ in both method and query syntax, filter, project, sort, group and join sequences, and understand why a query does nothing until it is enumerated.

**Objectives**

- Write the same query in method syntax and in query syntax
- Filter, project and sort with `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy` and `ThenBy`
- Group a sequence with `GroupBy` and combine two sequences with `Join`
- Explain deferred execution and predict when a query's code runs

**Outline**

1. What LINQ is
2. Method syntax and query syntax
3. Filtering, projecting and sorting
4. Grouping
5. Joining
6. Deferred execution

#### Lesson 11: LINQ in Practice

*30 minutes.* Summarise sequences with aggregation operators, build dictionaries and lookups, pick single elements safely, test sequences with `Any` and `All`, and avoid the hidden cost of enumerating a query twice.

**Objectives**

- Compute counts, sums, averages, minimums and maximums, and predict what each does on an empty sequence
- Build a `Dictionary` with `ToDictionary` and an `ILookup` with `ToLookup`, and explain how they treat duplicate and missing keys
- Choose between `First`, `FirstOrDefault` and `Single`, and between `Any`, `All` and `Count`
- Spot code that enumerates a deferred query more than once and fix it with `ToList`

**Outline**

1. Aggregation
2. Dictionaries and lookups
3. Removing duplicates
4. Picking one element
5. `Any` and `All`
6. The cost of enumerating twice

#### Lesson 12: Pattern Matching

*30 minutes.* Test the type, value and shape of data in one expression with type, property, positional, relational, logical and list patterns, and compute results with exhaustive switch expressions.

**Objectives**

- Test a value's run-time type and name the result with `is` and declaration patterns
- Write switch expressions with relational and logical patterns, case guards and a discard arm
- Match nested data with property, extended property and positional patterns
- Match arrays and lists by length and content with list and slice patterns, and read warning CS8509

**Outline**

1. Patterns, `is` and switch expressions
2. Type patterns
3. Relational and logical patterns
4. Property and positional patterns
5. List patterns
6. Exhaustiveness

#### Lesson 13: Extension Methods and Extension Members

*25 minutes.* Add methods, properties, static members and operators to types you cannot change, with classic extension methods and the extension blocks of C# 14, and see how LINQ is built from them.

**Objectives**

- Write a classic extension method with `this` and call it with instance syntax
- Predict which method a call binds to when the type and an extension declare the same member
- Declare an extension block with instance methods, extension properties and static extension members
- Decide when an extension is the right tool and when a method on the type itself is better

**Outline**

1. Adding members to types you do not own
2. Classic extension methods
3. How extension calls bind
4. Extension blocks in C# 14
5. LINQ is made of extensions
6. When to use extensions

#### Practice labs

One small lab per lesson, offered at the end of the lesson and checked in the sandbox like any other lab.

| After the lesson | Practice lab | What the learner does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structs, Enums and Tuples | Bakery Boxes | Give a readonly struct its computed property, ToString and Deconstruct, test and clear allergen flags, check an enum value that came from outside, and return two numbers as a tuple. |
| Value and Reference Semantics | Car Park Gate | Override Equals and GetHashCode so that a HashSet treats two spellings of a number plate as one car, and use a ref parameter to replace a struct the caller holds. |
| Inheritance and Polymorphism | Hotel Bill | Derive three kinds of room from an abstract base class, override the members each one changes, build on the base versions with base, and total a bill through base-class variables. |
| Interfaces | Race Results | Write a default interface method, implement an interface in a struct, give a class IComparable and IEquatable so that Sort and Contains work, and pick a winner from any mix of entries. |
| Records and Immutability | Theatre Booking | Turn a class into a readonly record struct, give a record a computed property, make changed copies with with expressions, and keep a record's list from being shared by its copies. |
| Properties and Encapsulation | Vending Machine | Validate two properties with the field keyword, make a credit that only its own class can change, add an indexer over private slots, and restock through a reference that may be null. |
| Generics | Animal Shelter | Write a generic method that needs an interface constraint, one that needs none and compares with EqualityComparer, and a generic class whose base-class and new() constraints let it create its animals. |
| Collections and Their Interfaces | Restaurant Kitchen | Cook orders from a queue, expose what was served through a read-only wrapper that stays current, and count dishes from any sequence into a sorted dictionary with a case-insensitive comparer. |
| Delegates and Lambdas | Photo Filters | Pass a filter into a method as a delegate, build new filters from lambdas that capture their arguments, chain several into one, and keep a count between calls in a closure. |
| LINQ Fundamentals | Farmers' Market | Filter and sort a market's sales with a tie-breaker, group them into quantities per product, join them with the stalls they came from, and return a query that runs only when it is read. |
| LINQ in Practice | Fitness Club | Summarise a week of workouts without failing on an empty one, total the minutes per member into a dictionary, pick the longest workout safely, and test every workout while reading the input only once. |
| Pattern Matching | Smart Home Hub | Classify temperatures with relational patterns, describe messages of any type with type, property and positional patterns, and parse spoken commands with list patterns, each as one switch expression. |
