#### Mock exam: Types, Generics and LINQ Mock Exam

*26 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from a larger bank on value and reference types, records, inheritance, interfaces, generics, collections, delegates, LINQ, pattern matching and extension members.

**Question 1** · One answer · `csharp-medium-01`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var a = Access.Read | Access.Delete;
Console.WriteLine(a);
Console.WriteLine((int)a);

[Flags]
enum Access { None = 0, Read = 1, Write = 2, Delete = 4 }
```

- **✔ A. `Read, Delete`, then `5`**
- B. `5`, then `5`
- C. `Delete`, then `4`, because the larger flag wins
- D. `Read | Delete`, then `5`

> **Why:** `|` combines the bits of `Read` (1) and `Delete` (4), giving the value 5. Because the enum is
> marked `[Flags]`, `ToString` lists every member contained in the value, separated by a comma
> and a space: `Read, Delete`. Without `[Flags]`, 5 matches no single member and would print as
> `5`. Nothing is lost when flags are combined, so no flag "wins", and `ToString` never prints
> C# operators such as `|`.

**Question 2** · One answer · `csharp-medium-02`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var level = (Level)7;
Console.WriteLine($"{level} {(int)Level.High} {default(Level)}");

enum Level { Low = 1, Medium, High }
```

- **✔ A. `7 3 0`**
- B. `High 3 Low`
- C. `7 3 Low`
- D. Nothing; the cast `(Level)7` throws `InvalidCastException`

> **Why:** Any integer can be cast to an enum, defined or not, and a value with no matching member prints
> as its number, so the first part is `7`. Members count up from the previous value, so `Medium`
> is 2 and `High` is 3. The default value of every enum is the all-zero value, `(Level)0`, even
> when no member has that value; it prints as `0`, not `Low`, because `Low` is 1. This is why an
> enum should have a sensible member for 0, and why numbers from outside should be checked with
> `Enum.IsDefined`.

**Question 3** · One answer · `csharp-medium-03`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var a = new Counter { Value = 1 };
var b = a;
b.Value = 5;
var list = new List<Counter> { a };
var c = list[0];
c.Value = 9;
Console.WriteLine($"{a.Value} {b.Value} {list[0].Value}");

struct Counter { public int Value; }
```

- **✔ A. `1 5 1`**
- B. `5 5 9`
- C. `1 5 9`
- D. `5 5 1`

> **Why:** `Counter` is a struct, a value type, so every assignment copies the whole value. `b = a` makes an
> independent copy, so changing `b` leaves `a` at 1. Adding `a` to the list stores another copy,
> and reading `list[0]` hands out yet another copy, so changing `c` does not touch the element
> in the list. With a class, all of these variables would share one object and the program would
> print `9 9 9`. To change a struct stored in a list, change a copy and assign it back with
> `list[0] = c;`, or better, make the struct immutable.

**Question 4** · Select all that apply · `csharp-medium-04`

Which statements about equality in C# are true? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. For a class that overrides nothing, `a == b` is `false` for two separate objects that hold the same data**
- **✔ B. Overriding `Equals` without `GetHashCode` can make `HashSet<T>.Contains` return `false` for an object that `Equals` says is in the set**
- C. `==` compiles for any struct and compares every field
- D. `ReferenceEquals(5, 5)` is `true` because the two values are equal

> **Why:** A plain class uses reference equality: `==` and `Equals` ask whether two references point at
> the same object. Hash-based collections pick a bucket with `GetHashCode` before calling
> `Equals`, so equal objects must have equal hash codes; with the default, identity-based hash
> code, an equal object is looked for in the wrong bucket. A struct gets value equality through
> `Equals`, but no `==` operator unless it declares one (`a == b` is error CS0019; records and
> tuples are the exceptions). `ReferenceEquals` takes `object` parameters, so each `5` is boxed
> into its own object, and two different boxes are never the same reference.

**Question 5** · One answer · `csharp-medium-05`

What happens when this program runs?

```csharp
int n = 10;
object o = n;
n++;
long big = (long)o;
Console.WriteLine($"{n} {big}");
```

- A. It prints `11 10`
- B. It prints `11 11`
- **✔ C. It throws `InvalidCastException` at `(long)o`**
- D. It does not compile, because an `object` cannot be cast to `long`

> **Why:** `object o = n` boxes the value: a new object holding a *copy* of 10, so `n++` would not affect
> it. The program never gets to print, though. Unboxing must name the exact type that was boxed.
> The box holds an `int`, and asking for a `long` throws `InvalidCastException` ("Unable to cast
> object of type 'System.Int32' to type 'System.Int64'"), even though an `int` converts to a
> `long` implicitly. The compiler accepts the cast because an `object` *might* hold a boxed
> `long`. The fix is `(long)(int)o`: unbox to `int`, then convert.

**Question 6** · One answer · `csharp-medium-06`

What does this program print?

```csharp
Base b = new Derived();
Console.WriteLine($"{b.A()} {b.B()} {((Derived)b).B()}");

class Base
{
    public virtual string A() => "base-A";
    public string B() => "base-B";
}

class Derived : Base
{
    public override string A() => "derived-A";
    public new string B() => "derived-B";
}
```

- **✔ A. `derived-A base-B derived-B`**
- B. `derived-A derived-B derived-B`
- C. `base-A base-B derived-B`
- D. `base-A base-B base-B`

> **Why:** `A` is virtual and `Derived` overrides it, so a call through a `Base` variable still runs the
> version for the object's run-time type: `derived-A`. `B` is not virtual; `Derived` *hides* it
> with `new`. For a hidden member, the variable's compile-time type decides, so `b.B()` runs
> `Base.B` and the same object cast to `Derived` runs `Derived.B`. One object giving two answers
> is why hiding is rarely what you want; use `virtual` and `override` for polymorphism.

**Question 7** · Select all that apply · `csharp-medium-07`

Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. An abstract class can have constructors and fully implemented methods**
- **✔ B. A non-abstract class that derives from an abstract class must override every abstract member it inherits**
- C. A sealed class can be used as a base class as long as it declares no virtual members
- D. A `protected` member can be used by any code in the same project

> **Why:** An abstract class is an incomplete base: it cannot be instantiated, but it can contain
> constructors (run by derived constructors through `base(...)`), fields and ordinary methods
> alongside its abstract members. Any concrete derived class must override all of those abstract
> members, or the compiler reports CS0534. `sealed` forbids derivation completely, whatever the
> class contains (CS0509). `protected` means "this class and derived classes"; access for all code
> in the same assembly is what `internal` means.

**Question 8** · One answer · `csharp-medium-08`

What happens when you build this program?

```csharp
var bot = new Bot();
IGreeter greeter = bot;
Console.WriteLine(greeter.Greet());
Console.WriteLine(bot.Greet());

interface IGreeter
{
    string Name { get; }
    string Greet() => $"Hello, {Name}";
}

class Bot : IGreeter
{
    public string Name => "R2";
}
```

- A. It builds and prints `Hello, R2` twice
- **✔ B. It fails with error CS1061 on `bot.Greet()`: a default interface method can be called only through the interface type**
- C. It fails because `Bot` does not implement the interface member `Greet`
- D. It builds, and the second line prints an empty string because `Bot` has no `Greet` of its own

> **Why:** `Greet` has a body in the interface, so it is a **default interface method**: `Bot` satisfies
> the interface without writing it. The default implementation belongs to the interface, not to
> the class, so it is reachable only through an expression of type `IGreeter`. `greeter.Greet()`
> is fine; `bot.Greet()` has static type `Bot`, which has no such member, so the compiler reports
> CS1061. Either call it through the interface or give `Bot` its own public `Greet`.

**Question 9** · One answer · `csharp-medium-09`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var jobs = new List<Job> { new Job("b", 1), new Job("a", 3), new Job("c", 3) };
jobs.Sort();
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", jobs.Select(j => j.Name)));

class Job : IComparable<Job>
{
    public Job(string name, int priority) { Name = name; Priority = priority; }
    public string Name { get; }
    public int Priority { get; }

    public int CompareTo(Job? other)
    {
        if (other is null) return 1;
        int byPriority = other.Priority.CompareTo(Priority);
        return byPriority != 0 ? byPriority : string.CompareOrdinal(Name, other.Name);
    }
}
```

- **✔ A. `a c b`**
- B. `b a c`
- C. `c a b`
- D. `b c a`

> **Why:** `Sort()` with no arguments uses `CompareTo`. A negative result puts this instance first.
> Comparing `other.Priority` with `Priority`, the reverse of the usual order, sorts the highest
> priority first, so both priority-3 jobs come before `b`. On a tie, the names are compared in
> the normal direction, so `a` comes before `c`. Swapping the receiver and the argument is the
> standard way to reverse one key while keeping the others ascending.

**Question 10** · One answer · `csharp-medium-10`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var p = new Point(1, 2);
var q = p with { Y = 5 };
var r = q with { Y = 2 };
Console.WriteLine($"{p == r} {ReferenceEquals(p, r)} {q}");

record Point(int X, int Y);
```

- **✔ A. `True False Point { X = 1, Y = 5 }`**
- B. `False False Point { X = 1, Y = 5 }`
- C. `True True Point { X = 1, Y = 5 }`
- D. Nothing; it fails to compile because positional record properties are read-only and `with` cannot change them

> **Why:** A `with` expression copies the record into a **new** object and then sets the listed
> properties; positional properties are `init`, which `with` is allowed to set. `r` ends up with
> the same values as `p`, and records generate value equality, so `p == r` is `True`, while
> `ReferenceEquals` confirms that they are different objects. The generated `ToString` prints the
> type name and every property in braces.

**Question 11** · True or false · `csharp-medium-11`

True or false: in the code below, the `with` expression gives `copy` its own new list, so
adding to `copy.Members` does not change `team.Members`.

```csharp
var team = new Team("Blue", new List<string> { "Ada" });
var copy = team with { Name = "Red" };
copy.Members.Add("Grace");

record Team(string Name, List<string> Members);
```

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** False. A `with` expression makes a **shallow** copy: it copies each property's value, and the
> value of a reference-type property is a reference. Both records point at the same
> `List<string>`, so after the `Add`, `team.Members` has two names as well. `init` only stops
> the property from being pointed at another list; it does not freeze the list. For deep
> immutability, store immutable or read-only collections, or create a new list explicitly:
> `team with { Members = new List<string>(team.Members) }`.

**Question 12** · One answer · `csharp-medium-12`

What does this C# 14 program print?

```csharp
int calls = 0;
Box? a = new Box();
Box? b = null;
a?.Size = -5;
b?.Size = Log(3);
a?.Size += 2;
Console.WriteLine($"{a?.Size} {calls}");

int Log(int value) { calls++; return value; }

class Box
{
    public int Size { get; set => field = Math.Max(0, value); }
}
```

- **✔ A. `2 0`**
- B. `-3 1`
- C. `2 1`
- D. Nothing; `?.` cannot appear on the left of an assignment

> **Why:** The setter uses the C# 14 `field` keyword to store into the compiler's backing field, and it
> clamps negative values to 0, so `a?.Size = -5` stores 0 and `a?.Size += 2` makes it 2. C# 14
> also allows `?.` on the left of `=` and compound assignments: when the receiver is `null`, the
> whole assignment is skipped, **including the right-hand side**, so `Log` is never called for
> `b` and `calls` stays 0. Only `++` and `--` are not allowed in this form.

**Question 13** · Select all that apply · `csharp-medium-13`

A class `Engine` is compiled into one assembly. A class `TurboEngine : Engine` is written in a
*different* assembly. Which members of `Engine` can code inside `TurboEngine` use? Select all
that apply.

- **✔ A. A `protected` member**
- **✔ B. A `protected internal` member**
- C. A `private protected` member
- D. An `internal` member

> **Why:** `protected` opens a member to derived classes wherever they are. `protected internal` is the
> *union* of `protected` and `internal`: derived classes anywhere, or any code in the same
> assembly. `private protected` is the *intersection*: derived classes, but only those in the
> same assembly, so `TurboEngine` is excluded. `internal` means the same assembly only, and
> being a derived class does not help.

**Question 14** · One answer · `csharp-medium-14`

Given this method:

```csharp
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T> => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
```

Which call fails to compile?

- A. `Max(3, 7)`
- B. `Max("apple", "pear")`
- **✔ C. `Max(new object(), new object())`**
- D. `Max(2.5, 1.0)`

> **Why:** The constraint `where T : IComparable<T>` lets the body call `CompareTo` and, in return,
> requires every type argument to implement `IComparable<T>`. `int`, `string` and `double` all
> do, and the compiler infers `T` from the arguments. `object` does not, so the call fails with
> error CS0311: "There is no implicit reference conversion from 'object' to
> 'System.IComparable<object>'". The mistake is caught at compile time, which is the point of
> generics over methods that take `object` and cast.

**Question 15** · One answer · `csharp-medium-15`

Why does this method not compile?

```csharp
static bool Same<T>(T a, T b) => a == b;
```

- **✔ A. `==` is not defined for every possible `T`, so the compiler rejects it (CS0019)**
- B. A generic method cannot return `bool`
- C. `T` must be given explicitly at the call site before `==` can be used
- D. Generic methods must be declared inside a generic class

> **Why:** Inside a generic method, the compiler allows only operations that are valid for *every* type
> `T` could be. Not every type has an `==` operator (a struct without one does not), so error
> CS0019 follows. Use `EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals(a, b)`, which works for any `T` and
> uses `IEquatable<T>` when it is available, or add a constraint that provides what you need.
> Note that `where T : class` would make `==` compile but compare references only.

**Question 16** · One answer · `csharp-medium-16`

What happens when this program runs?

```csharp
ICollection<int> items = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };
items.Add(4);
Console.WriteLine(items.Count);
```

- A. It prints `4`
- B. It does not compile, because arrays do not implement `ICollection<T>`
- **✔ C. It compiles, and `Add` throws `NotSupportedException`**
- D. It prints `3`, because `Add` is silently ignored for arrays

> **Why:** Arrays implement `ICollection<T>` and `IList<T>`, so the assignment compiles. But an array has a
> fixed size, so its `Add` throws `NotSupportedException` with "Collection was of a fixed size."
> An interface promises the member exists, not that every implementation supports it; check
> `IsReadOnly` (true for arrays) when it matters. If a method needs to add items, ask for a type
> that really supports it, such as `List<T>`, or return a new collection instead.

**Question 17** · One answer · `csharp-medium-17`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var actions = new List<Func<int>>();
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
{
    actions.Add(() => i * 10);
}
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", actions.Select(f => f())));
```

- A. `0,10,20`
- **✔ B. `30,30,30`**
- C. `20,20,20`
- D. Nothing; a lambda cannot use a loop variable

> **Why:** A lambda captures the **variable**, not its value at the time the lambda is created. A `for`
> loop has a single `i` for the whole loop, so all three lambdas share it, and they run only
> after the loop has finished, when `i` is 3. A `foreach` loop is different: it creates a fresh
> variable on each pass, so the same code with `foreach` over `0, 1, 2` prints `0,10,20`. To fix
> the `for` version, copy `i` into a local inside the loop body and capture the copy.

**Question 18** · One answer · `csharp-medium-18`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var names = new List<string> { "ada", "bo" };
var shortNames = names.Where(n => n.Length <= 2);
names.Add("cy");
var snapshot = shortNames.ToList();
names.Add("di");
Console.WriteLine($"{shortNames.Count()} {snapshot.Count}");
```

- A. `1 1`
- B. `2 2`
- **✔ C. `3 2`**
- D. `3 3`

> **Why:** `Where` uses deferred execution: `shortNames` stores the query, not its results, and reads
> `names` each time it is enumerated. `ToList()` runs it once, after `cy` was added, and keeps
> the two matches `bo` and `cy` in a new list that never changes. `Count()` runs the query again
> at the end, when `di` is there too, so it finds three. Use `ToList` or `ToArray` when you need
> a fixed snapshot.

**Question 19** · One answer · `csharp-medium-19`

The intent is to sort by age and then, for equal ages, by name. What does this print?

```csharp
var people = new[] { ("bo", 30), ("ada", 25), ("cy", 25) };
var sorted = people.OrderBy(p => p.Item2).OrderBy(p => p.Item1);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", sorted.Select(p => p.Item1)));
```

- A. `ada cy bo`
- **✔ B. `ada bo cy`**
- C. `cy ada bo`
- D. Nothing; `OrderBy` cannot follow `OrderBy`

> **Why:** A second `OrderBy` starts a completely new sort by its own key, so the result is ordered by
> name only: `ada bo cy`. The age order survives only among items with equal names, because the
> sort is stable. The intended result, `ada cy bo`, needs `ThenBy`, which adds a tie-breaker to
> the previous ordering: `people.OrderBy(p => p.Item2).ThenBy(p => p.Item1)`.

**Question 20** · Select all that apply · `csharp-medium-20`

`int[] empty = [];` Which of these calls throw an exception? Select all that apply.

- A. `empty.Sum()`
- **✔ B. `empty.Max()`**
- **✔ C. `empty.First()`**
- D. `empty.FirstOrDefault()`

> **Why:** `Sum` of nothing is 0, a meaningful answer. `Max` (like `Min` and `Average`) of an empty
> sequence of numbers has no meaningful answer, so it throws `InvalidOperationException`
> ("Sequence contains no elements"). `First` throws for the same reason when there is no element.
> `FirstOrDefault` returns `default(int)`, which is 0, instead of throwing; for an `int` that 0
> cannot be told apart from a real element, so pass your own fallback, as in
> `FirstOrDefault(-1)`, when the difference matters.

**Question 21** · True or false · `csharp-medium-21`

True or false: `numbers.All(n => n > 100)` returns `false` when `numbers` is an empty sequence.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** False. `All` returns `true` unless it finds an element that fails the test, and an empty
> sequence has no element to fail, so the answer is `true`. This is called being *vacuously*
> true. It surprises people in checks such as "all payments are cleared", which then pass when
> there are no payments at all. If an empty input should count as a failure, write
> `numbers.Any() && numbers.All(...)`, materializing the sequence first if it is a query.

**Question 22** · One answer · `csharp-medium-22`

What does this program print?

```csharp
Console.WriteLine($"{Kind(500)}|{Kind("hey")}|{Kind(2.0)}|{Kind(null)}");

static string Kind(object? o) => o switch
{
    int n when n > 100 => "big int",
    int => "int",
    string { Length: > 3 } s => $"long {s}",
    string => "short string",
    null => "null",
    _ => "other",
};
```

- **✔ A. `big int|short string|other|null`**
- B. `big int|long hey|other|null`
- C. `int|short string|other|other`
- D. `big int|short string|other|other`

> **Why:** Arms are tried from top to bottom. 500 is an `int` and the guard `n > 100` holds, so the first
> arm wins. `"hey"` is a string of length 3, which fails `{ Length: > 3 }`, so it falls to the
> plain `string` arm. `2.0` is a `double`, which matches no type arm and reaches the discard.
> Type patterns never match `null`, so `null` passes them all and is caught by the constant
> pattern `null` before the discard.

**Question 23** · One answer · `csharp-medium-23`

Which expression is `true` exactly when the `char c` is **not** a lowercase ASCII letter?

- A. `c is not >= 'a' and <= 'z'`
- **✔ B. `c is not (>= 'a' and <= 'z')`**
- C. `c is not 'a' or 'z'`
- D. `c is < 'a' and > 'z'`

> **Why:** `not` binds more tightly than `and`, which binds more tightly than `or`. The first option
> therefore means `(not >= 'a') and <= 'z'`: it is false for `{` and every other character above
> `z`, which are not lowercase letters either. The compiler hints at the problem with warning
> CS9336, "The pattern is redundant". The third means `(not 'a') or 'z'`, true for almost
> everything. The fourth can never be true, since no character is both below `a` and above `z`.
> The parentheses in the second option make `not` apply to the whole range.

**Question 24** · One answer · `csharp-medium-24`

`int[] v = [1, 2, 3, 4];` Which of these patterns does **not** match `v`?

- A. `v is [1, ..]`
- B. `v is [.., 3, 4]`
- C. `v is [_, _, ..]`
- **✔ D. `v is [1, _, 4]`**

> **Why:** A list pattern without a slice matches only sequences of exactly its length. `[1, _, 4]` has
> three elements, so it rejects any array of four. The slice pattern `..` matches zero or more
> elements, which is why `[1, ..]` (starts with 1), `[.., 3, 4]` (ends with 3, 4) and
> `[_, _, ..]` (at least two elements) all match. To say "starts with 1 and ends with 4", write
> `[1, .., 4]`.

**Question 25** · One answer · `csharp-medium-25`

What does this program print?

```csharp
var r = new Report();
Console.WriteLine($"{r.Title()} {r.Footer()}");

class Report
{
    public string Title() => "own";
}

static class ReportExtensions
{
    public static string Title(this Report r) => "extension";
    public static string Footer(this Report r) => "ext-footer";
}
```

- **✔ A. `own ext-footer`**
- B. `extension ext-footer`
- C. Nothing; the compiler reports that the call to `Title` is ambiguous
- D. Nothing; extension methods must be declared in a `public` class

> **Why:** The compiler first looks for a matching member on the type itself and considers extension
> methods only when there is none. `Report` has its own `Title()`, so that wins and the extension
> with the same signature is silently ignored; an extension can add behaviour but never replace
> it. `Footer` exists only as an extension, so it is used. The static class may be internal, as
> here; it must be static, non-generic and not nested.

**Question 26** · Select all that apply · `csharp-medium-26`

Which of these can a C# 14 `extension` block declare for a type you do not own? Select all
that apply.

- **✔ A. An extension property, such as `public bool IsEmpty => !source.Any();`**
- **✔ B. A static extension member called on the type itself, such as `TimeSpan.FromWorkDays(2)`**
- **✔ C. A user-defined operator, such as `+` for two values of the extended type**
- D. An instance field that stores extra data inside each object of the extended type

> **Why:** Extension blocks extend the old `this` syntax, which allowed only instance methods, with
> extension properties, static extension members (in a block whose receiver has no name) and
> operators. They are still static code compiled into the enclosing static class: they can
> compute from the receiver's accessible members, but they cannot add storage to the extended
> type, so an extension property can only be computed, never backed by a field of its own.

#### Lab: Library Loans Desk

*C# · about 50 minutes · 5 s per test.* Build the fines rules, a generic waitlist for reserved items and the LINQ reports behind a public library's loans desk.

**Scenario**

The Riverside branch library lends books, DVDs and magazines to about four thousand members.
Its loans desk still runs on a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet is losing: fines are worked out
by hand, the waiting list for popular DVDs lives on sticky notes, and nobody can say at a glance
how many items are out.

Each loan is already exported as a small record:

```text
member M02 (child)  DVD       due 2026-03-07  not yet returned
member M01 (adult)  book      due 2026-03-01  returned 2026-03-06
```

You are writing the core of the replacement service, as plain C# that the web front end will
call. It has three parts. The **fine rules** turn one loan into an amount owed. A **waitlist**
keeps members in the order they reserved a title; the library will use it for DVDs, for
inter-library requests keyed by tuples, and for whatever comes next, so it must be generic. The
**reports** answer the questions the desk asks every morning: what is overdue, who owes what,
and how many items of each kind are out.

The loans come from a database cursor that can be read only once, so the reports must not read
their input twice.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.cs`. The starter declares every type and signature; replace each
`throw new NotImplementedException();` with your code. Keep every type in the global namespace
(no `namespace` line) and do not change `MemberKind`, `ItemKind` or `Loan`.

```csharp
public enum MemberKind { Adult, Child, Senior, Staff }
public enum ItemKind { Book, Dvd, Magazine }

// Returned is null while the item is still out.
public readonly record struct Loan(
    string MemberId, MemberKind Member, ItemKind Item, DateOnly Due, DateOnly? Returned = null);
```

1. **`Fines.For(Loan loan, DateOnly today)`** returns the fine for one loan as a `decimal`.
   - A returned loan is charged up to its `Returned` date; a loan still out is charged up to
     `today`.
   - Days late is that date minus `Due`, in whole days. If it is zero or less, the fine is `0`.
   - The daily rate is `0.20` for a `Book`, `1.00` for a `Dvd` and `0.10` for a `Magazine`.
   - A `Child` or a `Senior` pays half the daily rate. `Staff` never pay. An `Adult` pays the full
     rate.
   - A single loan's fine, after any discount, never exceeds `10.00`.
2. **`Waitlist<T>`**, where `T : notnull`, keeps members in the order they joined. Two members
   are the same if `T`'s own equality says so.
   - `int Count` is the number of members waiting.
   - `bool Join(T member)` adds the member at the back and returns `true`. If the member is
     already waiting, it changes nothing and returns `false`.
   - `bool Leave(T member)` removes the member and returns `true`, or returns `false` if the member
     was not waiting.
   - `T Next()` removes and returns the member at the front. On an empty waitlist it throws
     `InvalidOperationException`.
   - `int PositionOf(T member)` is the member's place in the line, starting at `1` for the front,
     or `0` if the member is not waiting.
   - `int RemoveAll(Predicate<T> match)` removes every waiting member for which `match` returns
     `true`, keeps the others in order, and returns how many it removed.
   - `Waitlist<T>` implements `IEnumerable<T>`, listing the members from front to back.
3. **`LoanReports`** holds three extension members on `IEnumerable<Loan>`. The starter writes them
   in a C# 14 extension block; you may use classic extension methods for the two methods instead,
   as long as the calls below still work. Each of them reads `loans` **at most once**: the input
   may be a stream that cannot be read twice.
   - `loans.Overdue(today)` returns the loans that are still out and whose `Due` is before
     `today`, earliest `Due` first; loans due on the same day are ordered by `MemberId` (ordinal).
     A loan due today is not overdue.
   - `loans.FinesByMember(today)` returns an `IReadOnlyList<(string MemberId, decimal Total)>`:
     one entry per member, the total of `Fines.For` over that member's loans. Members whose total
     is `0` are left out. The largest total comes first; equal totals are ordered by `MemberId`
     (ordinal).
   - `loans.OpenByKind` is a property returning an `IReadOnlyDictionary<ItemKind, int>`: the
     number of loans still out for **every** `ItemKind`, including kinds with none out.

Example:

```csharp
var today = new DateOnly(2026, 3, 10);
Loan[] loans =
[
    new Loan("M01", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, new DateOnly(2026, 3, 1), new DateOnly(2026, 3, 6)),
    new Loan("M02", MemberKind.Child, ItemKind.Dvd, new DateOnly(2026, 3, 7)),
    new Loan("M01", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Dvd, new DateOnly(2026, 2, 1), new DateOnly(2026, 3, 3)),
    new Loan("M03", MemberKind.Staff, ItemKind.Dvd, new DateOnly(2026, 3, 2)),
    new Loan("M04", MemberKind.Senior, ItemKind.Magazine, new DateOnly(2026, 3, 9)),
    new Loan("M02", MemberKind.Child, ItemKind.Book, new DateOnly(2026, 3, 20)),
];

Fines.For(loans[0], today);   // 1.00   5 days x 0.20
Fines.For(loans[1], today);   // 1.50   3 days x 0.50, still out
Fines.For(loans[2], today);   // 10.00  30 days x 1.00, capped

loans.Overdue(today);         // M03 (due 2 March), M02 (7 March), M04 (9 March)
loans.FinesByMember(today);   // [("M01", 11.00), ("M02", 1.50), ("M04", 0.05)]
loans.OpenByKind;             // Book 1, Dvd 2, Magazine 1

var holds = new Waitlist<string>();
holds.Join("M01");            // true
holds.Join("M02");            // true
holds.Join("M01");            // false: already waiting
holds.PositionOf("M02");      // 2
holds.Next();                 // "M01"
string.Join(",", holds);      // "M02"
```

**Tips.** `DateOnly.DayNumber` turns a date into a whole number of days. A switch expression
keeps the rate rules readable. `Enum.GetValues<ItemKind>()` lists every kind. If you count with
LINQ, remember that every `Count(...)` over `loans` is another read.

    string MemberId, MemberKind Member, ItemKind Item, DateOnly Due, DateOnly? Returned = null);

// ---- 1. Fine rules -----------------------------------------------------------------------

public static class Fines
{
    /// <summary>The fine owed for one loan, checked on <paramref name="today"/>.</summary>

// ---- 2. A generic waitlist ---------------------------------------------------------------

/// <summary>Members waiting for something, in the order they joined.</summary>
public class Waitlist<T> : IEnumerable<T> where T : notnull
{
    // TODO 2: choose the field(s) that keep the waiting members in order.

    public int Count => throw new NotImplementedException();

    /// <summary>Adds the member at the back; false if the member is already waiting.</summary>
    public bool Join(T member) => throw new NotImplementedException();

    /// <summary>Removes the member; false if the member was not waiting.</summary>
    public bool Leave(T member) => throw new NotImplementedException();

    /// <summary>Removes and returns the member at the front.</summary>
    public T Next() => throw new NotImplementedException();

    /// <summary>1 for the front of the line, 0 if the member is not waiting.</summary>
    public int PositionOf(T member) => throw new NotImplementedException();

    /// <summary>Removes every member that matches; returns how many were removed.</summary>
    public int RemoveAll(Predicate<T> match) => throw new NotImplementedException();

    /// <summary>The waiting members, front to back.</summary>
    public IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator() => throw new NotImplementedException();

    // The non-generic interface that IEnumerable<T> extends; it can reuse the method above.
    System.Collections.IEnumerator System.Collections.IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => GetEnumerator();
}

// ---- 3. Reports, as extension members on any sequence of loans -----------------------------

public static class LoanReports
{
    extension(IEnumerable<Loan> loans)
    {
        /// <summary>Loans still out and due before today; earliest due first, then by member.</summary>
        public IEnumerable<Loan> Overdue(DateOnly today) => throw new NotImplementedException();

        /// <summary>Each member's total fine, largest first; members owing nothing left out.</summary>
        public IReadOnlyList<(string MemberId, decimal Total)> FinesByMember(DateOnly today) =>
            throw new NotImplementedException();

        /// <summary>How many loans are still out, for every item kind.</summary>
        public IReadOnlyDictionary<ItemKind, int> OpenByKind => throw new NotImplementedException();
    }
}
```

Check.Equal(Fines.For(loans[0], today), 1.00m, "fine for a book returned 5 days late by an adult");
Check.Equal(Fines.For(loans[1], today), 1.50m, "fine for a DVD a child still has, 3 days late");
Check.Equal(Fines.For(loans[2], today), 10.00m, "fine for a DVD returned 30 days late");

Check.SequenceEqual(
    loans.Overdue(today).Select(loan => loan.MemberId),
    new[] { "M03", "M02", "M04" },
    "members with overdue loans, earliest due date first");

Check.SequenceEqual(
    loans.FinesByMember(today),
    new[] { ("M01", 11.00m), ("M02", 1.50m), ("M04", 0.05m) },
    "total fine per member, largest first");

var open = loans.OpenByKind;
Check.Equal(open[ItemKind.Book], 1, "books still out");
Check.Equal(open[ItemKind.Dvd], 2, "DVDs still out");
Check.Equal(open[ItemKind.Magazine], 1, "magazines still out");

var holds = new Waitlist<string>();
Check.True(holds.Join("M01"), "M01 joins an empty waitlist");
Check.True(holds.Join("M02"), "M02 joins behind M01");
Check.True(!holds.Join("M01"), "Join returns false for a member who is already waiting");
Check.Equal(holds.PositionOf("M02"), 2, "position of the second member in line");
Check.Equal(holds.Next(), "M01", "Next serves the front of the line");
Check.Equal(string.Join(",", holds), "M02", "the members still waiting, front to back");
```

**Test 2: Applies every fine rule, including dates, discounts and the cap** (hidden)

```csharp
// Every fine rule on its own. All loans are due on 10 May 2026.
var due = new DateOnly(2026, 5, 10);
var later = new DateOnly(2026, 6, 30);

decimal Fine(MemberKind member, ItemKind item, DateOnly? returned, DateOnly today) =>
    Fines.For(new Loan("X1", member, item, due, returned), today);

// Dates.
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, due, later), 0m,
    "a loan returned on its due date");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, due.AddDays(-3), later), 0m,
    "a loan returned before its due date");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, due.AddDays(2), later), 0.40m,
    "a returned loan is charged up to its return date, not up to today");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, null, due.AddDays(7)), 1.40m,
    "a loan still out is charged up to today");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, null, due), 0m,
    "a loan still out on its due date");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, null, due.AddDays(-1)), 0m,
    "a loan still out that is not yet due");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, new DateOnly(2026, 6, 2), later), 4.60m,
    "days late counted across the end of a month");

// Rates by item.
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, due.AddDays(1), later), 0.20m,
    "daily rate for a book");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(2), later), 2.00m,
    "daily rate for a DVD");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Magazine, due.AddDays(4), later), 0.40m,
    "daily rate for a magazine");

// Shares by member.
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Child, ItemKind.Book, due.AddDays(3), later), 0.30m,
    "what a child pays for a late book");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Senior, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(3), later), 1.50m,
    "what a senior pays for a late DVD");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Staff, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(40), later), 0m,
    "what staff pay for a very late DVD");

// The cap.
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(10), later), 10.00m,
    "a fine of exactly the cap");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(11), later), 10.00m,
    "a fine just above the cap");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Child, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(25), later), 10.00m,
    "the cap is applied after the discount");
Check.Equal(Fine(MemberKind.Child, ItemKind.Dvd, due.AddDays(16), later), 8.00m,
    "a discounted fine that stays below the cap");
```

**Test 3: Keeps a waitlist in order for any member type** (hidden)

```csharp
// A waitlist of ints: the container must not assume strings.
var line = new Waitlist<int>();
Check.Equal(line.Count, 0, "a new waitlist is empty");
Check.Equal(line.PositionOf(7), 0, "PositionOf for a member who is not waiting");
Check.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => line.Next(), "Next on an empty waitlist");
Check.True(!line.Leave(7), "Leave for a member who is not waiting");

Check.True(line.Join(7), "Join for a new member");
Check.True(line.Join(3), "Join for a second new member");
Check.True(!line.Join(7), "Join for a member who is already waiting");
Check.Equal(line.Count, 2, "Count after a refused Join");
Check.True(line.Join(9), "Join for a third new member");
Check.SequenceEqual(line, new[] { 7, 3, 9 }, "members are listed in the order they joined");

Check.True(line.Leave(3), "Leave for a waiting member");
Check.True(!line.Leave(3), "Leave for a member who has already left");
Check.Equal(line.PositionOf(9), 2, "positions after a member in front leaves");
Check.Equal(line.Next(), 7, "Next serves the member who joined first");
Check.Equal(line.Count, 1, "Count after Next");
Check.Equal(line.PositionOf(7), 0, "a member served by Next is no longer waiting");
Check.True(line.Join(7), "a member served by Next can join again");
Check.SequenceEqual(line.ToList(), new[] { 9, 7 }, "a member who joins again goes to the back");
Check.Equal(line.Next(), 9, "Next after a member rejoined");
Check.Equal(line.Next(), 7, "Next serves the last member");
Check.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => line.Next(), "Next after the waitlist has been emptied");

// Tuple members: equality comes from the member type.
var requests = new Waitlist<(string Id, bool Suspended)>();
foreach (string id in new[] { "P1", "P2", "P3", "P4", "P5" })
{
    requests.Join((id, id is "P2" or "P4"));
}
Check.True(!requests.Join(("P3", false)), "Join for a value equal to one already waiting");
Check.Equal(requests.PositionOf(("P5", false)), 5, "PositionOf finds a member by value");

int removed = requests.RemoveAll(request => request.Suspended);
Check.Equal(removed, 2, "the number RemoveAll returns");
Check.SequenceEqual(requests.Select(request => request.Id), new[] { "P1", "P3", "P5" },
    "the members RemoveAll keeps, in order");
Check.Equal(requests.RemoveAll(request => request.Suspended), 0, "RemoveAll when nothing matches");
Check.Equal(requests.Count, 3, "Count after RemoveAll");
Check.True(requests.Join(("P2", true)), "a member removed by RemoveAll can join again");
Check.Equal(requests.PositionOf(("P2", true)), 4, "where a rejoining member is placed");
```

**Test 4: Orders the reports, handles empty input and reads the loans once** (hidden)

```csharp
// Ties, exclusions, empty input and reading the input only once.
var today = new DateOnly(2026, 9, 15);
DateOnly Sept(int day) => new DateOnly(2026, 9, day);

List<Loan> loans =
[
    new Loan("B7", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, Sept(10)),                // out, owes 1.00
    new Loan("A2", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Magazine, Sept(5)),             // out, owes 1.00
    new Loan("C1", MemberKind.Staff, ItemKind.Dvd, Sept(1)),                  // out, owes nothing
    new Loan("Z9", MemberKind.Senior, ItemKind.Dvd, Sept(12), Sept(14)),      // returned, owes 1.00
    new Loan("A2", MemberKind.Child, ItemKind.Book, Sept(15)),                // out, due today
    new Loan("M5", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Dvd, Sept(13)),                 // out, owes 2.00
    new Loan("A1", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, Sept(10)),                // out, owes 1.00
    new Loan("Q4", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, Sept(1), Sept(1)),        // returned on time
];

Check.SequenceEqual(
    loans.Overdue(today).Select(loan => loan.MemberId),
    new[] { "C1", "A2", "A1", "B7", "M5" },
    "overdue loans: only unreturned loans due before today, by due date and then member id");

Check.SequenceEqual(
    loans.FinesByMember(today),
    new[] { ("M5", 2.00m), ("A1", 1.00m), ("A2", 1.00m), ("B7", 1.00m), ("Z9", 1.00m) },
    "fines per member: members owing nothing left out, equal totals ordered by member id");

var open = loans.OpenByKind;
Check.Equal(open.Count, 3, "OpenByKind has an entry for every item kind");
Check.Equal(open[ItemKind.Book], 3, "books still out, including one due today");
Check.Equal(open[ItemKind.Dvd], 2, "DVDs still out, not counting returned ones");
Check.Equal(open[ItemKind.Magazine], 1, "magazines still out");

// No loans at all.
var none = new List<Loan>();
Check.True(!none.Overdue(today).Any(), "Overdue with no loans");
Check.Equal(none.FinesByMember(today).Count, 0, "FinesByMember with no loans");
Check.Equal(none.OpenByKind.Count, 3, "OpenByKind lists every item kind even with no loans");
Check.True(none.OpenByKind.Values.All(count => count == 0), "OpenByKind counts with no loans");

// Only staff and returned-on-time loans: nobody owes anything.
Loan[] nothingOwed =
[
    new Loan("S1", MemberKind.Staff, ItemKind.Dvd, Sept(1)),
    new Loan("S2", MemberKind.Adult, ItemKind.Book, Sept(1), Sept(1)),
];
Check.Equal(nothingOwed.FinesByMember(today).Count, 0, "FinesByMember when every total is zero");

// The input is a stream: each report may read it only once.
int reads = 0;
IEnumerable<Loan> Stream()
{
    reads++;
    foreach (Loan loan in loans)
    {
        yield return loan;
    }
}

var streamed = Stream().FinesByMember(today);
Check.Equal(reads, 1, "how many times FinesByMember read its input");
Check.Equal(streamed.Count, 5, "FinesByMember over a stream");

reads = 0;
var openStreamed = Stream().OpenByKind;
Check.Equal(reads, 1, "how many times OpenByKind read its input");
Check.Equal(openStreamed[ItemKind.Book], 3, "OpenByKind over a stream");

reads = 0;
var overdueStreamed = Stream().Overdue(today).ToList();
Check.Equal(reads, 1, "how many times one enumeration of Overdue read its input");
Check.Equal(overdueStreamed.Count, 5, "Overdue over a stream");
```
