#### Mock exam: Shell Foundations Mock Exam

*25 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from the level's bank, from first commands and paths to permissions, redirection, searching and shell configuration.

**Question 1** · One answer · `linux-basic-01`

A colleague says a server runs "Debian 12 with Linux 6.1". What is Linux 6.1 in that
sentence?

- A. The version of the distribution, which Debian then renames for its own release
- **✔ B. The version of the kernel, the core program that manages the hardware and runs every other program**
- C. The version of the Bash shell that Debian installs by default
- D. The version of the GNU core utilities, such as `ls` and `cp`

> **Why:** Strictly speaking, Linux is a **kernel**. Debian 12 is the **distribution**: the kernel plus
> the GNU tools, thousands of other programs, an installer and a package manager, released
> together. The shell (Bash) and the core utilities come from the GNU project and have their
> own version numbers, which is why the whole system is also called GNU/Linux.

**Question 2** · One answer · `linux-basic-02`

What does this line print in an interactive Bash shell? (`whoaim` is a typing mistake for
`whoami`.)

```bash
whoaim && echo done; echo $?
```

- A. `bash: whoaim: command not found`, then `done`, then `0`
- B. `bash: whoaim: command not found`, then `0`
- **✔ C. `bash: whoaim: command not found`, then `127`**
- D. Nothing at all, because the whole line is rejected before anything runs

> **Why:** The shell finds no command called `whoaim`, prints the error and records exit status
> **127**, the shell's code for "command not found". `&&` runs the next command only after a
> success, so `echo done` is skipped. `;` runs the next command whatever happened, and
> `echo $?` prints the status of the last command that ran, the failed lookup. The status is
> not 0: zero means success.

**Question 3** · One answer · `linux-basic-03`

You want the manual page that describes the **format of the file** `/etc/passwd`, not the
`passwd` command. What do you type?

- A. `man passwd`
- B. `man /etc/passwd`
- C. `passwd --help`
- **✔ D. `man 5 passwd`**

> **Why:** The manual is divided into sections: 1 for user commands, 5 for file formats, 8 for
> administration commands. `passwd` has a page in both 1 and 5, and `man passwd` shows the
> first match, the command in section 1. Putting the section number first, `man 5 passwd`,
> selects the file format. `passwd --help` documents the command, and `man /etc/passwd`
> does not look up a page by that name. `whatis passwd` lists both pages with their sections.

**Question 4** · Select all that apply · `linux-basic-04`

The synopsis of `cp` includes this form:

```text
cp [OPTION]... SOURCE... DIRECTORY
```

Which commands fit this form? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `cp a.txt b.txt backup/`**
- **✔ B. `cp -v -i notes.txt archive/`**
- C. `cp backup/`
- D. `cp [-v] notes.txt archive/`

> **Why:** Square brackets mark something **optional**, `...` means **may be repeated**, and words
> without brackets are **required**. So any number of options (including none), then one or
> more sources, then exactly one directory. `cp a.txt b.txt backup/` has two sources, and
> `cp -v -i notes.txt archive/` has two options and one source. `cp backup/` has no source.
> The brackets are notation, never typed: `cp [-v] ...` passes a literal `[-v]` as a file
> name.

**Question 5** · One answer · `linux-basic-05`

What does this sequence print?

```bash
cd /home/dana/projects/website
cd ../..
pwd
```

- A. `/home/dana/projects`
- **✔ B. `/home/dana`**
- C. `/home`
- D. `../..`

> **Why:** `..` is the parent directory, so `../..` climbs two levels: from `website` to `projects`,
> then to `dana`. `pwd` always prints an absolute path, starting at `/`, never the relative
> path you typed. One `..` would have stopped at `/home/dana/projects`.

**Question 6** · One answer · `linux-basic-06`

Your home directory contains `.bashrc`, `.profile` and `notes.txt`. Which command lists all
three, but not the `.` and `..` entries?

- A. `ls -a`
- B. `ls -l`
- **✔ C. `ls -A`**
- D. `ls *`

> **Why:** Names that begin with a dot are **hidden**: `ls` skips them unless asked. `-a` shows
> everything, including the `.` (this directory) and `..` (parent) entries; `-A` ("almost
> all") shows hidden files but leaves those two out. `-l` changes the format, not the
> selection. `ls *` lists only what the shell's `*` matched, and `*` does not match names
> that start with a dot.

**Question 7** · One answer · `linux-basic-07`

`backup` is an **existing** directory. Where does this command put the copy of
`site/css/main.css`?

```bash
cp -r site backup
```

- A. `backup/css/main.css`
- **✔ B. `backup/site/css/main.css`**
- C. Nowhere: `cp` refuses because `backup` already exists
- D. `backup/main.css`, because `-r` flattens the tree

> **Why:** When the destination is an existing directory, `cp` (and `mv`) put the source **inside**
> it, keeping its name, so the tree arrives as `backup/site/...`. Only if `backup` did not
> exist would `cp -r` create it as the copy itself, giving `backup/css/main.css`. Running
> the same command twice therefore gives different results, which is why `-v` (show each
> copy) is worth adding when unsure.

**Question 8** · Select all that apply · `linux-basic-08`

`old` is an **empty** directory. Which commands remove it? Select all that apply.

- A. `rm old`
- **✔ B. `rmdir old`**
- C. `rm -f old`
- **✔ D. `rm -r old`**

> **Why:** `rmdir` removes empty directories, and `rm -r` removes a directory with everything in it,
> so both work here. Plain `rm` does not remove directories at all: it fails with
> `rm: cannot remove 'old': Is a directory`. `-f` only silences missing files and prompts;
> it does not add the ability to remove directories, so `rm -f old` fails the same way.
> Prefer `rmdir` when a directory should be empty: if it is not, it refuses.

**Question 9** · One answer · `linux-basic-09`

A file was written without a newline after its last line:

```bash
printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma' > f.txt
wc -l f.txt
```

What does `wc -l` print?

- A. `3 f.txt`
- B. `0 f.txt`
- **✔ C. `2 f.txt`**
- D. An error, because the file does not end with a newline

> **Why:** `wc -l` counts **newline characters**, not visible lines. There are two `\n` in the file,
> after `alpha` and after `beta`, so it reports 2, although three lines appear when you
> `cat` it. Most programs end every line properly, but files from hand-written tools
> sometimes do not, and this is how counts end up one short. `wc -w` would still report 3
> words.

**Question 10** · One answer · `linux-basic-10`

A directory contains `img-1.png`, `img-2.png`, `img-10.png`, `img-a.png` and `.img-3.png`.
What does this print?

```bash
echo img-?.png
```

- A. `img-1.png img-2.png img-10.png img-a.png`
- **✔ B. `img-1.png img-2.png img-a.png`**
- C. `img-1.png img-2.png`
- D. `img-1.png img-2.png .img-3.png img-a.png`

> **Why:** `?` matches exactly **one** character of any kind, so it matches `1`, `2` and `a` but not
> the two characters `10`. `.img-3.png` does not start with `img-`, and a leading dot must
> be matched explicitly in any case. Only `[0-9]` would restrict the match to digits. The
> shell does the matching before `echo` runs, which is why `echo` is the safe way to preview
> a pattern.

**Question 11** · One answer · `linux-basic-11`

For user `dana`, what does this print?

```bash
echo '$HOME is' "$HOME" \$HOME
```

- **✔ A. `$HOME is /home/dana $HOME`**
- B. `/home/dana is /home/dana /home/dana`
- C. `$HOME is $HOME $HOME`
- D. `'$HOME is' /home/dana \$HOME`

> **Why:** Single quotes keep everything literal, so `'$HOME is'` stays as written. Double quotes
> still expand `$`, so `"$HOME"` becomes `/home/dana`. The backslash protects the next
> character, so `\$HOME` prints a literal `$HOME`. The quotes and the backslash themselves
> are removed by the shell before `echo` runs, which is why none of them is printed.

**Question 12** · One answer · `linux-basic-12`

In `/home/dana/proj` there is a file `guide.txt` and a directory `docs`. You run:

```bash
cd /home/dana/proj
ln -s guide.txt docs/guide-link
cat docs/guide-link
```

What happens?

- **✔ A. `cat` fails with `No such file or directory`: the link points to `docs/guide.txt`**
- B. `cat` prints `guide.txt`, because a link's content is a path
- C. `ln` refuses to create a link in a different directory from its target
- D. `cat` prints the contents of `guide.txt`, because the target is resolved from where you ran `ln`

> **Why:** A symbolic link stores its target as text and resolves it later **relative to the
> directory the link is in**. This link lives in `docs`, so `guide.txt` means
> `docs/guide.txt`, which does not exist: the link is broken (dangling). Write the target from
> the link's point of view, `ln -s ../guide.txt docs/guide-link`, or use an absolute path.
> `readlink docs/guide-link` would show the stored text, `guide.txt`; `cat` follows the
> link, it does not print it.

**Question 13** · True or false · `linux-basic-13`

True or false: after these commands, the text `data` is gone, because `a.txt` was the
original file.

```bash
echo data > a.txt
ln a.txt b.txt
rm a.txt
```

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** `ln` without `-s` makes a **hard link**: a second name for the same inode. Neither name is
> the original. `rm` removes one name and lowers the link count from 2 to 1; the data is
> only released when the count reaches zero. `cat b.txt` still prints `data`. With a
> symbolic link (`ln -s`) the statement would be true in effect: the link would be broken.

**Question 14** · One answer · `linux-basic-14`

Which permission string does `chmod 750 deploy.sh` give?

- A. `rwxrw----`
- B. `rw-r-x---`
- **✔ C. `rwxr-x---`**
- D. `---r-xrwx`

> **Why:** Each digit is the sum of `r` = 4, `w` = 2, `x` = 1, and the digits are owner, group,
> others, in that order. 7 = 4+2+1 = `rwx`, 5 = 4+1 = `r-x`, 0 = `---`. So the owner may do
> everything, the group may read and run the script, and others get nothing. `rwxrw----`
> would be 760, and reading the digits from the right would put the owner last, which is
> never the order.

**Question 15** · Select all that apply · `linux-basic-15`

Which statements about permissions on a **directory** are true? Select all that apply.

- A. Making a file read-only with `chmod a-w` stops its owner from deleting it
- **✔ B. Deleting a file needs write permission on the directory that contains it**
- **✔ C. Without `x` on a directory you cannot `cd` into it or open the files inside it**
- D. `644` is a sensible mode for a directory that others should be able to browse

> **Why:** A directory is a list of names. `w` lets you change the list (create, rename, delete
> entries), so deletion depends on the **directory's** `w`, not the file's: in a writable
> directory you can delete a read-only file. `x` lets you enter the directory and use the
> entries in it; with `r` but no `x` you can see names but not open them. That is why `644`
> (no `x` for anyone) makes a directory unusable; directories normally want `755` or `750`.

**Question 16** · One answer · `linux-basic-16`

`/etc/hostname` exists and `/nowhere` does not. What appears on the **terminal**?

```bash
ls /etc/hostname /nowhere 2>&1 > out.txt
```

- **✔ A. Only the error, `ls: cannot access '/nowhere': No such file or directory`**
- B. Nothing; both the output and the error go into `out.txt`
- C. Only `/etc/hostname`
- D. Both lines, and `out.txt` stays empty

> **Why:** Redirections are processed **left to right**. `2>&1` first points stderr at wherever stdout
> goes *at that moment*, the terminal. Then `> out.txt` moves stdout to the file. So the
> error still reaches the screen and the file holds only `/etc/hostname`. To send both to
> the file, put the file first: `> out.txt 2>&1`, or use `&> out.txt`.

**Question 17** · One answer · `linux-basic-17`

`names.txt` holds two lines, `b` and `a`. What is in `names.txt` after this command?

```bash
sort names.txt > names.txt
```

- A. `a` and `b`, in that order
- **✔ B. Nothing; the file is empty**
- C. `b` and `a`, unchanged, because `sort` notices the conflict and stops
- D. The four lines `a`, `b`, `b`, `a`

> **Why:** The shell sets up `> names.txt` **before** `sort` starts, and `>` empties an existing file.
> By the time `sort` opens `names.txt` to read it, the file is already empty, so there is
> nothing to sort and nothing to write. Sort into a new file and then replace the old one:
> `sort names.txt > sorted.txt && mv sorted.txt names.txt`.

**Question 18** · One answer · `linux-basic-18`

`app.log` exists and contains no line with `refund`. What is the exit status of this
command?

```bash
grep refund app.log
```

- A. `0`, because `grep` ran without problems
- B. `2`
- **✔ C. `1`**
- D. `127`

> **Why:** `grep` uses its exit status to report the search result: **0** if at least one line
> matched, **1** if no line matched, **2** if an error occurred, such as a file that does
> not exist. A search that finds nothing prints nothing, so the status is the only way to
> tell "nothing found" from "something went wrong". 127 is the shell's "command not found".

**Question 19** · Select all that apply · `linux-basic-19`

`app.log` contains these four lines:

```text
Error one
warning two
error three
ERRORS: 0
```

Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `grep -ci error app.log` prints `3`**
- B. `grep error app.log` prints `Error one` and `error three`
- **✔ C. `grep -wi error app.log` prints `Error one` and `error three`**
- D. `grep -v error app.log` prints only `warning two`

> **Why:** `-i` ignores case, so `error`, `Error` and `ERRORS` all match, and `-c` counts the 3
> matching lines. `-w` requires a whole word, which excludes `ERRORS`. Without `-i`, `grep
> error` matches only the lower-case `error three`. `-v` inverts the match, and without `-i`
> it prints every line that lacks lower-case `error`: `Error one`, `warning two` and
> `ERRORS: 0`.

**Question 20** · One answer · `linux-basic-20`

The current directory contains `a.log` and `b.log`, and a subdirectory with `c.log`. Why
does this command fail with `find: paths must precede expression`?

```bash
find . -name *.log
```

- **✔ A. The shell expanded `*.log` to `a.log b.log` before `find` ran, so `find` received an extra argument**
- B. `find` needs `-type f` before `-name`
- C. `-name` only accepts exact names, not wildcards
- D. The starting point `.` must be written as `./`

> **Why:** Unquoted wildcards are expanded by the **shell**, in the current directory, before the
> command starts. `find` therefore received `-name a.log b.log`, and `b.log` is not a valid
> part of an expression. Quote the pattern, `find . -name '*.log'`, so that `find` receives
> the `*` and applies it to every name in the tree, including `sub/c.log`. With exactly one
> matching file the command would not even fail; it would silently search for that one name.

**Question 21** · One answer · `linux-basic-21`

In vi you changed a file by mistake, typed `:q` and Enter, and saw
`E37: No write since last change (add ! to override)`. You want to leave and **keep the
file as it was on disk**. What do you type?

- A. `:wq` then Enter
- **✔ B. `:q!` then Enter**
- C. `ZZ`
- D. Ctrl+X, then `N`

> **Why:** `:q` refuses to quit while the buffer has unsaved changes; adding `!` overrides that and
> discards them. `:wq` and `ZZ` both **write** the changed buffer first, which is the
> opposite of what you want. Ctrl+X then `N` is how you leave **nano** without saving; in vi
> it does nothing useful. If you are not sure which mode you are in, press Esc first.

**Question 22** · One answer · `linux-basic-22`

What does the last line print?

```bash
colour=blue
export size=large
bash -c 'echo "colour=[$colour] size=[$size]"'
```

- A. `colour=[blue] size=[large]`
- B. `colour=[] size=[]`
- **✔ C. `colour=[] size=[large]`**
- D. `colour=[blue] size=[]`

> **Why:** `bash -c` starts a **child** process. A child receives only the **environment**, that is,
> variables marked with `export`. `size` was exported, so the child sees it; `colour` is a
> plain shell variable and stays in the parent. The single quotes matter too: they stop the
> parent shell from expanding the variables, so the child does the expanding.

**Question 23** · True or false · `linux-basic-23`

True or false: Bash looks in the current directory for commands, so an executable script
`tool.sh` in the working directory can be run by typing just `tool.sh`.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** A command name without a `/` is looked up as an alias, function or builtin, and then in
> the directories of `PATH`, in order. The current directory is normally **not** in
> `PATH`, so `tool.sh` gives `command not found`. Run it with a path, `./tool.sh`, or add
> its directory to `PATH`. Leaving `.` out is deliberate: otherwise a file named like a
> common command, placed in a shared directory, could run in its place.

**Question 24** · One answer · `linux-basic-24`

After `umask 077`, which permissions do a new file made with `touch` and a new directory
made with `mkdir` get?

- **✔ A. File `rw-------` (600), directory `rwx------` (700)**
- B. File `rwx------` (700), directory `rwx------` (700)
- C. File `---rwxrwx` (077), directory `---rwxrwx` (077)
- D. File `rw-r--r--` (644), directory `rwxr-xr-x` (755)

> **Why:** The umask lists bits to **remove**. Programs normally ask for `666` for files and `777`
> for directories; removing `077` (everything for group and others) leaves `600` and `700`.
> Files never get `x` from the default, which is why scripts need `chmod +x`. `644` and `755`
> are what the common umask `022` produces.

**Question 25** · One answer · `linux-basic-25`

The directory contains `big report.txt` and `report.txt`. What happens with this command?

```bash
rm big report.txt
```

- A. It deletes `big report.txt` only
- **✔ B. It prints an error for `big` and deletes `report.txt`, leaving `big report.txt`**
- C. Nothing is deleted, because one of the names does not exist
- D. It deletes both files

> **Why:** The shell splits the line at spaces, so `rm` receives two names, `big` and `report.txt`.
> It reports `rm: cannot remove 'big': No such file or directory` and goes on to delete
> `report.txt`, the wrong file. `rm` handles each argument independently, so one missing name
> does not stop the others. Quote names with spaces: `rm "big report.txt"`.

#### Lab: Field Station Data Release

*Bash · about 45 minutes · 5 s per test.* Turn a messy data-logger upload into a tidy, read-only release folder with a README link and a summary, using only the commands of this level.

**Scenario**

You look after the computers of a small ecology research group. Out at Field Station 7, a data
logger measures air temperature and soil moisture three times a day, and once a week it uploads
everything it has into a single folder: readings as CSV files, its own log files, a few notes,
and whatever else it happened to leave behind, such as a rotated old log, a backup file, a
hidden state file and a placeholder for a camera image.

The researchers do not want to dig through that folder. They want each upload turned into a
tidy **release folder**: readings in one place, logs in another, notes in a third; data that
cannot be changed by accident; logs that only you can open; a `README.txt` at the top; and a
short summary that says at a glance how many files arrived and how many errors the logger
reported.

This week's upload is waiting for you in `data/`. Here is `ls -A data`:

```text
.upload-state.txt  2026-10-07.csv  calibration.txt  logger.log.1
2026-10-05.csv     README.txt      field-notes.txt  photo-0412.jpg
2026-10-06.csv     backup.csv.bak  logger.log       upload.log
```

Uploads from other stations arrive in folders whose names contain spaces, such as
`uploads/site B`, so your script must cope with those too. You will run it every week, so it
has to get every detail right without supervision.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.sh`. It is run with two arguments, the upload folder and the release folder to
create:

```bash
bash solution.sh data release-week41
bash solution.sh "uploads/site B" "out/week 42/release"
```

The starter already stores them in the variables `upload` and `release`. Either path may
contain spaces, so always write them in double quotes: `"$upload"`, `"$release"/logs`.

1. **Folders.** Create the release folder with three subfolders: `readings`, `logs` and
   `notes`. Create any missing parent folders too. All three subfolders must exist even if
   nothing is copied into them.
2. **Copy, by name.** From the top level of the upload folder only (not its subfolders), copy:
   - every file whose name ends in `.csv` into `readings`;
   - every file whose name ends in `.log` into `logs`;
   - every file whose name ends in `.txt` into `notes`.

   Hidden files (names starting with `.`) are not copied, and neither is anything else, such as
   `logger.log.1` or `backup.csv.bak`. Copy; never move or change the upload folder. File names
   may contain spaces.
3. **Permissions.**
   - Every file in `readings` and `notes` must be read-only for everyone: mode `444`
     (`r--r--r--`).
   - The `logs` folder must be private to you: mode `700` (`rwx------`).
   - The `readings` and `notes` folders themselves keep the mode `mkdir` gives them, `755`.
4. **README link.** Every upload contains `README.txt`. In the release folder, create a symbolic
   link called `README.txt` whose target is exactly `notes/README.txt`, so that it keeps working
   when the whole release folder is moved or renamed.
5. **Summary.** Print exactly these four lines, and save the same four lines in the file
   `SUMMARY.txt` in the release folder:

   ```text
   readings: <number of files in readings>
   logs: <number of files in logs>
   notes: <number of files in notes>
   errors: <number of lines in the copied log files that contain ERROR>
   ```

   `ERROR` must be in capital letters: a line that says `error` in lower case does not count.
6. **Quiet and successful.** An upload with no CSV files or no log files is normal. In that case
   copy nothing of that kind, report `0`, and do not print anything on standard error. The
   script must always finish with exit status `0`.

For `data/` the output is:

```text
readings: 3
logs: 2
notes: 3
errors: 3
```

**Tools you have learned:** `mkdir`, `cp`, `chmod`, `ln`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, `wc`, `echo`,
wildcards, quoting, redirection (`>`, `>>`, `2>`, `/dev/null`), pipes, `tee` and `$( )`.

**Tips:**

- Put quotes around the variable but not around the wildcard: `"$upload"/*.csv`. Inside quotes,
  `*` is just a star.
- A pattern that matches nothing is passed on unchanged, and the command then complains about a
  file called `*.csv`. Decide where that complaint should go.
- A symbolic link's target is read from the folder the link is in, not from where you ran `ln`.
- Count with `ls FOLDER | wc -l`. `grep -c` gives one count per file when it reads several.

**Boilerplate given to the learner** (`starter.sh`)

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: bash solution.sh <upload-folder> <release-folder>
#
# Package one data-logger upload into a tidy release folder: readings, logs and
# notes copied by name, read-only data, a private logs folder, a README.txt link
# and a four-line summary. The instructions give every rule and the exact output.
set -u

upload="$1"     # the folder the logger uploaded, for example: data
release="$2"    # the release folder to create, for example: release-week41

# YOUR CODE 1: create "$release" with the subfolders readings, logs and notes.

# YOUR CODE 2: copy the .csv, .log and .txt files from the top of "$upload".

# YOUR CODE 3: make the files in readings and notes read-only (444),
#              and the logs folder private (700).

# YOUR CODE 4: create the symbolic link "$release/README.txt" -> notes/README.txt

# YOUR CODE 5: count the files and the ERROR lines, print the four summary
#              lines and save the same lines in "$release/SUMMARY.txt".
```

**Test cases the backend runs**

**Test 1: Packages the week 41 upload in data/** (visible)

```bash
expected='readings: 3
logs: 2
notes: 3
errors: 3'

actual=$(bash solution.sh data release-week41) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "the summary printed for the upload in data/"

[ -f release-week41/SUMMARY.txt ] || fail "release-week41/SUMMARY.txt was not created"
assert_eq "$(cat release-week41/SUMMARY.txt)" "$expected" "the contents of release-week41/SUMMARY.txt"

[ -L release-week41/README.txt ] || fail "release-week41/README.txt is not a symbolic link"
assert_eq "$(head -n 1 release-week41/README.txt)" "Field Station 7, upload for week 41." \
  "the first line read through the release-week41/README.txt link"
```

**Test 2: Copies exactly the right files, even with spaces in names, and leaves the upload untouched** (hidden)

```bash
site="uploads/site B"
mkdir -p "$site/old"
printf 'time,flow_l\n06:00,12\n' > "$site/north field.csv"
printf 'time,flow_l\n06:00,9\n' > "$site/south field.csv"
printf 'time,flow_l\n06:00,3\n' > "$site/old/last week.csv"
printf 'time,flow_l\n' > "$site/.partial.csv"
printf '06:00 ERROR pump 2 stalled\n06:05 INFO pump 2 restarted\n06:30 ERROR pump 2 stalled\n' > "$site/pump log.log"
printf '07:00 ERROR old entry\n' > "$site/old/archive.log"
printf 'Site B, week 42.\n' > "$site/README.txt"
printf 'Check the pump.\n' > "$site/to do.txt"
before=$(ls -AR "$site")

release="out/week 42/release"
actual=$(bash solution.sh "$site" "$release") || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"

expected='readings: 2
logs: 1
notes: 2
errors: 2'
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "the summary for an upload whose folder and file names contain spaces"

assert_eq "$(ls -A "$release/readings")" "north field.csv
south field.csv" "the files copied into readings (top level only, no hidden files)"
assert_eq "$(ls -A "$release/logs")" "pump log.log" "the files copied into logs (top level only)"
assert_eq "$(ls -A "$release/notes")" "README.txt
to do.txt" "the files copied into notes"
assert_eq "$(cat "$release/SUMMARY.txt" 2> /dev/null)" "$expected" "SUMMARY.txt holds the same four lines as the output"
assert_eq "$(ls -AR "$site")" "$before" "the upload folder is left exactly as it was"
```

**Test 3: Sets the permissions and a README link that survives moving the release** (hidden)

```bash
mkdir up3
printf 'Station 9 upload.\n' > up3/README.txt
printf 'time,temp_c\n06:00,4.2\n' > up3/morning.csv
printf 'time,temp_c\n18:00,6.0\n' > up3/evening.csv
printf '06:00 INFO ok\n' > up3/station.log
touch up3/empty.txt

bash solution.sh up3 rel3 > /dev/null || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"

for file in rel3/readings/morning.csv rel3/readings/evening.csv rel3/notes/README.txt rel3/notes/empty.txt; do
  [ -f "$file" ] || fail "$file was not copied"
  assert_eq "$(stat -c %a "$file")" "444" "the permissions of $file"
done
assert_eq "$(stat -c %a rel3/logs)" "700" "the permissions of the logs folder"
assert_eq "$(stat -c %a rel3/readings)" "755" "the permissions of the readings folder itself"
assert_eq "$(stat -c %a rel3/notes)" "755" "the permissions of the notes folder itself"

[ -L rel3/README.txt ] || fail "README.txt in the release folder is not a symbolic link"
assert_eq "$(readlink rel3/README.txt)" "notes/README.txt" "the target stored in the README.txt link"

mv rel3 "moved release"
assert_eq "$(cat "moved release/README.txt" 2> /dev/null)" "Station 9 upload." \
  "reading README.txt through the link after the release folder was moved"
```

**Test 4: Handles an upload with no readings and no logs quietly** (hidden)

```bash
mkdir quiet
printf 'Nothing was recorded this week: the logger was in for repair.\n' > quiet/README.txt

actual=$(bash solution.sh quiet rel4 2> errors4.txt) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status for an upload with no readings or logs"

expected='readings: 0
logs: 0
notes: 1
errors: 0'
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "the summary for an upload that holds only README.txt"
assert_eq "$(cat errors4.txt)" "" "standard error when the upload has no CSV or log files"

for folder in readings logs notes; do
  [ -d "rel4/$folder" ] || fail "rel4/$folder does not exist (the subfolders are needed even when empty)"
done
assert_eq "$(stat -c %a rel4/logs)" "700" "the permissions of an empty logs folder"
```

The reference solution is [`content/tracks/linux/basic/lab/solution.sh`](../content/tracks/linux/basic/lab/solution.sh).

### Level II · Medium: Text and Automation

Process text and automate work at the command line: the filters sort, uniq, cut, paste, tr and nl, regular expressions with grep, stream editing with sed, reports with awk, finding files with find and xargs, archives and compression, then shell scripts with variables, arguments, conditions and loops, managing processes and jobs, and installing software with apt, dpkg, dnf and rpm. The level ends with a lab that turns a folder of messy timesheets into a report.

**After this level you can**

- Build pipelines of filters, regular expressions, sed and awk that turn raw text into summaries and reports
- Find files by name, type, size, age and permissions, and act on them safely with -exec, -delete and xargs -0
- Create, inspect and extract tar, gzip, xz and zip archives, and verify them with checksums
- Write Bash scripts that take arguments, quote correctly, test conditions, loop over files and lines, and report an exit status
- Manage processes and jobs with ps, kill, bg, fg, nohup and nice, and install, query and remove packages on Debian and Red Hat systems

#### Lesson 1: Text Filters

*30 minutes.* Sort, count, cut, join, translate and number lines of text with the classic filter commands, then chain them into pipelines that answer real questions.

**Objectives**

- Sort lines as text, as numbers and by a chosen field with `sort -n`, `-r`, `-t` and `-k`
- Count and remove duplicate lines with `uniq` and `sort -u`, and explain why `uniq` needs sorted input
- Pick out, combine and change columns and characters with `cut`, `paste`, `tr` and `nl`
- Build a pipeline of filters that turns a raw file into a short summary

**Outline**

1. What a filter is
2. Sorting lines with `sort`
3. Sorting by a field
4. Duplicates: `uniq` and `sort -u`
5. Columns: `cut` and `paste`
6. Characters: `tr`

#### Mock exam: Text and Automation Mock Exam

*23 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from a larger bank on text filters, regular expressions, sed, awk, find and xargs, archives, shell scripts, conditions, loops, processes and package management.

**Question 1** · One answer · `linux-medium-01`

What does this command print?

```bash
printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort
```

- **✔ A. `10`, `100`, `9`, one per line**
- B. `9`, `10`, `100`, one per line
- C. `100`, `10`, `9`, one per line
- D. `9`, `100`, `10`, one per line

> **Why:** Without options, `sort` compares lines as text, one character at a time from the left. `10` and
> `100` both start with `1`, which sorts before `9`, and `10` is a prefix of `100`, so it comes
> first. Numeric order (`9 10 100`) needs `sort -n`, which compares the value of the leading
> number instead of its characters.

**Question 2** · One answer · `linux-medium-02`

`orders.csv` holds lines such as `ada,pen,3`: customer, product, quantity. Which pipeline
prints each product with the number of orders for it, most frequent first?

- **✔ A. `cut -d, -f2 orders.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`**
- B. `cut -d, -f2 orders.csv | uniq -c | sort -rn`
- C. `sort -t, -k2 orders.csv | uniq -c`
- D. `cut -d, -f2 orders.csv | sort -u | wc -l`

> **Why:** `uniq -c` only merges identical lines that are next to each other, so the products must be
> sorted first; the final `sort -rn` puts the largest counts on top. Without the first `sort`, a
> product that appears in separate places is counted in several pieces (`2 pen` and `1 pen`).
> Sorting whole lines by field 2 and counting them counts entire orders, which are all different.
> `sort -u | wc -l` counts how many different products there are, not how often each occurs.

**Question 3** · Select all that apply · `linux-medium-03`

Which commands print `orders.csv` (lines such as `ada,pen,3`) ordered by the quantity in the
third field, largest first? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `sort -t, -k3,3nr orders.csv`**
- **✔ B. `sort -t, -k3nr orders.csv`**
- C. `sort -t, -k3,3 -r orders.csv`
- D. `sort -k3,3nr orders.csv`

> **Why:** `-t,` makes the comma the field separator and `-k3,3nr` compares field 3 alone, as a number, in
> reverse. `-k3nr` runs from field 3 to the end of the line, but field 3 is the last field and
> `n` reads only the leading number, so it gives the same order here (write the end anyway; it is
> safer). Without `n`, the key is compared as text, and `3` sorts after `25`. Without `-t,`, the
> line contains no blanks, so it has a single field, field 3 is empty for every line and nothing
> is sorted by quantity.

**Question 4** · One answer · `linux-medium-04`

A file contains the four lines `ac`, `abc`, `abbc` and `ab+c`. What does this print?

```bash
grep 'ab+c' file
```

- **✔ A. `ab+c` only**
- B. `abc` and `abbc`
- C. `ac`, `abc` and `abbc`
- D. Nothing, because `+` is not valid in a pattern

> **Why:** Without `-E`, grep uses basic regular expressions, in which `+` is an ordinary character. The
> pattern therefore means the literal text `ab+c`. With `grep -E 'ab+c'`, `+` means "one or more of
> the previous item" and the command prints `abc` and `abbc`. In basic syntax the same operator is
> written `\+`. `ac` would match only `ab*c`, since `*` allows zero `b`s.

**Question 5** · Select all that apply · `linux-medium-05`

Which commands print the lines of `app.conf` that are neither comments (lines starting with
`#`) nor empty? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `grep -v '^#' app.conf | grep -v '^$'`**
- **✔ B. `grep -Ev '^(#|$)' app.conf`**
- C. `grep -v '#|^$' app.conf`
- D. `grep -v '^[#$]' app.conf`

> **Why:** `^#` matches a line that starts with `#`, and `^$` a line with nothing between its start and its
> end; `-v` keeps the lines that do not match. The extended pattern `^(#|$)` combines both. In
> basic syntax (no `-E`) `|` is a literal character, so `'#|^$'` looks for the text `#|` and
> removes almost nothing. `[#$]` is one character, `#` or `$`, so it removes comments and lines
> starting with a dollar sign, but an empty line has no character to match and stays.

**Question 6** · One answer · `linux-medium-06`

What does this print?

```bash
echo 'a-b-c' | sed 's/-/+/'
```

- **✔ A. `a+b-c`**
- B. `a+b+c`
- C. `a-b-c`
- D. `+`

> **Why:** The `s` command replaces only the first match on each line unless you add the `g` flag.
> `s/-/+/g` would print `a+b+c`, and `s/-/+/2` would replace only the second hyphen, printing
> `a-b+c`. The replacement takes the place of the matched text only; the rest of the line is kept.

**Question 7** · One answer · `linux-medium-07`

`config.txt` has three lines, `one`, `old value` and `three`. What does it contain after this
command?

```bash
sed -n -i 's/old/new/p' config.txt
```

- **✔ A. Only the line `new value`**
- B. `one`, `new value` and `three`
- C. `one`, `new value`, `new value` and `three`
- D. It is unchanged; sed refuses to combine `-n` with `-i`

> **Why:** `-i` replaces the file with whatever sed prints. `-n` turns off the automatic printing of every
> line, so the only output is what the `p` flag prints: the one line where a substitution
> happened. The other lines are lost. Drop `-n` and the `p` flag to edit in place safely, and add
> a backup suffix (`-i.bak`) so a mistake can be undone.

**Question 8** · One answer · `linux-medium-08`

What does this print?

```bash
printf 'a,1\nb,2\na,3\n' | awk -F, '{ t[$1] += $2 } END { for (k in t) print k, t[k] }' | sort
```

- **✔ A. `a 4` and `b 2`**
- B. `a 3` and `b 2`
- C. `a 1`, `b 2` and `a 3`
- D. `6`

> **Why:** `-F,` splits each line at the comma. `t[$1] += $2` adds the second field to the array entry for
> the first field, starting from zero the first time a key appears, so `a` collects 1 + 3 and `b`
> collects 2. The `END` loop prints one line per key; `sort` gives them a predictable order,
> because `for (k in t)` has none. With `=` instead of `+=`, the last value would win and `a`
> would show `3`.

**Question 9** · True or false · `linux-medium-09`

In awk, a variable must be set to 0 in a `BEGIN` block before an action such as
`total += $3` will work.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** awk variables need no declaration. A variable that has never been assigned counts as `0` in
> arithmetic and as the empty string in text, so `total += $3` simply starts from zero. `BEGIN` is
> useful for printing a header or setting `FS` and `OFS`, but not needed to start a total.

**Question 10** · One answer · `linux-medium-10`

A directory holds an empty file, a 1-byte file and a 500-byte file. Which of them does
`find . -type f -size -1k` list?

- **✔ A. Only the empty file**
- B. All three, since each is smaller than 1024 bytes
- C. The 1-byte and 500-byte files, but not the empty one
- D. None, because `-1k` is not a valid size

> **Why:** `find` rounds each file's size **up** to whole units before comparing. In kibibytes, the 1-byte
> and 500-byte files both count as 1k, and "less than 1k" leaves only files of size 0. To find
> files under 1024 bytes, compare in bytes: `-size -1024c`.

**Question 11** · Select all that apply · `linux-medium-11`

Which commands count the lines of every `.txt` file under `docs`, working correctly even for
a file named `my notes.txt`? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `find docs -name '*.txt' -print0 | xargs -0 wc -l`**
- **✔ B. `find docs -name '*.txt' -exec wc -l {} +`**
- C. `find docs -name '*.txt' | xargs wc -l`
- D. `wc -l $(find docs -name '*.txt')`

> **Why:** `-print0` ends every name with a null byte and `xargs -0` splits only there, so spaces and
> newlines in names survive. `-exec ... {} +` hands the names to `wc` directly, with no splitting
> at all. Plain `xargs` splits its input at blanks, and an unquoted `$(...)` is split by the
> shell, so both turn `docs/my notes.txt` into `docs/my` and `notes.txt`, and `wc` reports that
> neither exists.

**Question 12** · One answer · `linux-medium-12`

In a directory containing `notes.txt` and no other files, someone runs:

```bash
tar -czf notes.txt backup.tar.gz
```

What happens?

- **✔ A. `notes.txt` is overwritten with a new, empty compressed archive, and tar reports that `backup.tar.gz` does not exist**
- B. `backup.tar.gz` is created and holds `notes.txt`
- C. tar refuses to run because the archive name does not end in `.tar.gz`
- D. `notes.txt` is added to the existing `backup.tar.gz`

> **Why:** The word straight after `-f` is the archive to create, whatever its name, and the remaining
> words are the files to put in it. tar therefore creates `notes.txt` as the archive, replacing
> the original, and then fails to find `backup.tar.gz`. The correct order is
> `tar -czf backup.tar.gz notes.txt`. tar never checks that an archive's name matches its format.

**Question 13** · One answer · `linux-medium-13`

What is in the directory after running `gzip report.log`?

- **✔ A. `report.log.gz` only; the original file is replaced**
- B. `report.log` and `report.log.gz`
- C. `report.log`, now compressed but with the same name
- D. Nothing changes; gzip only prints compressed data unless given `-f`

> **Why:** `gzip` replaces each file it compresses with a `.gz` version, and `gunzip` does the reverse.
> To keep the original, add `-k`; to write the compressed data to standard output instead, use
> `-c`. `zcat report.log.gz` reads the content without decompressing it to disk.

**Question 14** · One answer · `linux-medium-14`

`args.sh` contains:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
for a in $@; do echo "[$a]"; done
```

What does `bash args.sh "two words" x` print?

- **✔ A. `[two]`, `[words]` and `[x]`, one per line**
- B. `[two words]` and `[x]`, one per line
- C. `[two words x]`
- D. `[$@]`

> **Why:** An unquoted `$@` expands to the arguments and then the shell splits the result at spaces, so
> `two words` becomes two items. Written as `"$@"`, each argument stays exactly one word, which
> gives `[two words]` and `[x]`. `"$*"` would join everything into one word, `[two words x]`.
> This is why every expansion of an argument or a file name should be in double quotes.

**Question 15** · One answer · `linux-medium-15`

A script contains the line `name = "Ada"`. What happens when it runs?

- **✔ A. The shell reports `name: command not found`, and `name` stays unset**
- B. `name` is set to `Ada`
- C. `name` is set to ` Ada`, with a leading space
- D. The line compares `name` with `Ada` and continues silently

> **Why:** An assignment is written with no spaces around `=`: `name="Ada"`. With spaces, the shell sees
> three words and runs the first, `name`, as a command with the arguments `=` and `Ada`. As no
> such command exists, it reports an error and carries on with the next line. Comparisons belong
> inside `[ ]` or `[[ ]]`.

**Question 16** · Select all that apply · `linux-medium-16`

The variable `count` holds `10`. Which commands correctly test whether it is greater than 9?
Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `[ "$count" -gt 9 ]`**
- **✔ B. `[[ $count -gt 9 ]]`**
- C. `[ "$count" > 9 ]`
- D. `[ "$count" \> 9 ]`

> **Why:** Numbers are compared with `-eq`, `-ne`, `-lt`, `-le`, `-gt` and `-ge`, in `[ ]` or `[[ ]]`.
> Inside `[ ]`, a bare `>` is a redirection: the test becomes `[ "$count" ]`, which is true for
> any non-empty value, and a file named `9` is created. Escaped as `\>`, it compares the values
> as **text**, and `10` sorts before `9`, so the test is false although 10 is greater.

**Question 17** · One answer · `linux-medium-17`

What does this print?

```bash
true && false || echo fallback
```

- **✔ A. `fallback`**
- B. Nothing, because the first command succeeded
- C. `true`
- D. An error, because `&&` and `||` cannot be combined

> **Why:** `&&` runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded, and `||` only if it failed. The
> chain is read from left to right: `true` succeeds, so `false` runs and fails, so `echo` runs.
> `a && b || c` is therefore not an if-else: `c` runs whenever `a` **or** `b` fails. When `b`
> can fail, write a real `if a; then b; else c; fi`.

**Question 18** · One answer · `linux-medium-18`

What does this print?

```bash
printf 'a\nb' > f
while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < f
```

- **✔ A. `a` only**
- B. `a` and `b`, one per line
- C. `b` only
- D. Nothing

> **Why:** The file's last line, `b`, has no newline after it. `read` still stores `b` in `line`, but
> returns a failure status because it reached the end of the file, so the loop stops before
> printing it. `while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]` lets that final line through, and also
> keeps leading spaces, which plain `read` removes.

**Question 19** · One answer · `linux-medium-19`

`f3` has three lines. What does this print?

```bash
count=0
cat f3 | while read -r l; do count=$((count + 1)); done
echo "$count"
```

- **✔ A. `0`**
- B. `3`
- C. `1`
- D. An error, because `count` is not visible inside the loop

> **Why:** Each command of a pipeline runs in a subshell, a separate copy of the shell. The loop counts to
> 3 in its own copy of `count`, and that copy disappears when the pipeline ends, leaving the
> original `0`. Redirecting the file into the loop, `done < f3`, keeps the loop in the current
> shell and prints `3`.

**Question 20** · One answer · `linux-medium-20`

Which signal does `kill 1234` send to process 1234?

- **✔ A. `TERM` (15), a request to finish**
- B. `KILL` (9), which cannot be ignored
- C. `HUP` (1), as if the terminal had closed
- D. `INT` (2), as if Ctrl+C had been pressed

> **Why:** With no signal named, `kill` sends `TERM`, which asks the program to finish and lets it clean up
> first. `kill -9` (`KILL`) ends it at once and cannot be caught; keep it for programs that ignore
> `TERM`. `HUP` is what a closing terminal sends and `INT` is what Ctrl+C sends.

**Question 21** · True or false · `linux-medium-21`

Pressing Ctrl+Z ends the foreground program, just as Ctrl+C does.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** Ctrl+Z sends `TSTP`, which **suspends** the program: it stays in memory, stopped, and `jobs`
> lists it as `Stopped`. `fg` resumes it in the foreground and `bg` lets it continue in the
> background. Ctrl+C sends `INT`, which normally ends the program.

**Question 22** · Select all that apply · `linux-medium-22`

Which commands tell you which installed package owns the file `/usr/bin/jq`? Select all that
apply.

- **✔ A. `dpkg -S /usr/bin/jq` on Debian or Ubuntu**
- **✔ B. `rpm -qf /usr/bin/jq` on Fedora or Red Hat**
- C. `dpkg -L /usr/bin/jq` on Debian or Ubuntu
- D. `apt install /usr/bin/jq` on Debian or Ubuntu

> **Why:** `dpkg -S` searches the installed packages' file lists for a path, and `rpm -qf` queries the
> package that owns a file. `dpkg -L` works the other way round: it takes a package name and lists
> its files, so given a path it fails with an error. `apt install` installs packages and is no
> way to ask a question.

**Question 23** · One answer · `linux-medium-23`

Why should a shell script call `apt-get` rather than `apt` to install packages?

- **✔ A. `apt`'s command-line interface and output may change between versions, while `apt-get` keeps backward compatibility**
- B. `apt` cannot install packages without a terminal
- C. Only `apt-get` resolves dependencies; `apt` installs single packages
- D. `apt` exists only on Ubuntu, `apt-get` on every Debian system

> **Why:** `apt` is designed for people at a terminal, and it says so: in a pipe it prints `WARNING: apt
> does not have a stable CLI interface. Use with caution in scripts.` Both tools resolve
> dependencies from the same repositories, and both exist on Debian and Ubuntu. Scripts use
> `apt-get` and `apt-cache`, usually with `-y` so the script does not stop at the confirmation
> question.

#### Lab: Timesheet Hours Report

*Bash · about 45 minutes · 5 s per test.* Turn a folder tree of messy staff timesheet exports into the hours-per-project report that finance invoices from.

**Scenario**

Larkspur Studio is a design studio of twelve people. Everyone records their hours per project,
and at the end of each month the office manager drops all the exports into one shared folder,
sorted by month and by person. Finance bills clients from the totals, and until now someone has
added them up by hand in a spreadsheet, which took a day and was wrong twice last quarter.

The exports come from three different places, and it shows:

```text
date,employee,project,hours
2026-09-01, Ben Okafor , BOREALIS , 8
2026-09-03,Ben Okafor,apollo,7,5
# 2026-09-03 was a public holiday
```

The spreadsheet on the office PC saves Windows line endings. The phone app never ends its files
with a newline. People type project names in any case, add spaces, leave comments, and now and
then write `7,5` for seven and a half hours. Other files land in the folder too: notes, backups,
old exports.

Finance wants a short report they can trust: the hours per project, the grand total, and how many
lines were rejected, so that someone can go and fix them before the invoices go out.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.sh`. It is run as `bash solution.sh DIRECTORY`.

1. **Arguments.** If no argument is given, or the argument is not a directory, print exactly
   `usage: solution.sh DIRECTORY` on standard error, print nothing on standard output, and exit
   with status `2`.
2. **Files.** Read every regular file whose name ends in `.csv` (lower case), in `DIRECTORY` or in
   any directory below it. Ignore every other file. File and directory names may contain spaces.
3. **Lines.** Every line of every file counts, including a last line that has no newline after
   it. A carriage return (`\r`) at the end of a line is not part of the line.
4. **Lines to skip.** Skip these lines without counting them anywhere:
   - blank lines: empty, or only spaces and tabs;
   - comments: the first character that is not a space or a tab is `#`;
   - headers: the first field, without the spaces around it, is exactly `date`.
5. **Records.** Every other line is a record, `date,employee,project,hours`, with fields
   separated by commas. Spaces and tabs at the start or end of a field are not part of it. A
   record is **valid** when all of these hold:
   - it has exactly four fields;
   - the date has the form `YYYY-MM-DD`: four digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, two digits;
   - the project is not empty;
   - the hours are one or more digits, optionally followed by a point and **one** digit. `8`,
     `7.5` and `0.5` are valid; `.5`, `7.25`, `-2`, `8h` and an empty field are not.

   Every record that is not valid is **rejected**.
6. **Projects.** Project names are not case-sensitive: `Apollo`, `APOLLO` and ` apollo ` are all
   the project `apollo`, and the report uses the lower-case name. Project names never contain
   spaces inside them.
7. **Report.** Print one line per project, `<project> <hours>`, with the hours of all its valid
   records added up and printed with exactly one decimal place. Put the project with the most
   hours first; projects with equal hours are ordered by name, as `sort` orders them. Then print
   two more lines: `total <hours>`, the hours of all valid records with one decimal place, and
   `rejected <count>`.
8. Exit with status `0` after printing the report, even when no file or no valid record was found.

For the sample folder `data/` (`bash solution.sh data`) the report is:

```text
apollo 22.5
borealis 14.0
cygnus 6.0
total 42.5
rejected 2
```

The two rejected lines are Ben's `7,5` (five fields) and `seven`. `README.txt` is not a
timesheet, whatever it contains.

**Tools available:** `bash`, `find`, `xargs`, `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`.

**Tips.**
- Build it in stages and look at the output of each: list the files, then print their lines,
  then clean the lines, then add up.
- Try your script on a folder of your own with awkward cases: a file name with a space, a file
  saved with `printf 'a,b\r\n'`, and a file whose last line has no newline. What does `cat` do
  with two such files?
- awk can do arithmetic with decimals and print them with `printf "%.1f"`; Bash arithmetic
  cannot.

**Boilerplate given to the learner** (`starter.sh`)

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: bash solution.sh DIRECTORY
#
# Report the hours per project in the timesheets (*.csv) under DIRECTORY,
# most hours first, then the total and the number of rejected lines.
set -u

# "${1-}" is the first argument, or an empty string when none was given.
dir="${1-}"

# YOUR CODE: if "$dir" is empty or not a directory, print the usage message on
# standard error and exit with status 2.

# YOUR CODE: find every regular *.csv file under "$dir" (names may contain
# spaces) and read all of their lines.

# YOUR CODE: remove carriage returns, skip blank lines, comments and headers,
# check each record, and add up the hours per project (in lower case).

# YOUR CODE: print "<project> <hours>" lines (most hours first, ties by name),
# then "total <hours>" and "rejected <count>".
```

**Test cases the backend runs**

**Test 1: Reports the sample timesheets** (visible)

```bash
expected='apollo 22.5
borealis 14.0
cygnus 6.0
total 42.5
rejected 2'

actual=$(bash solution.sh data) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status for the sample folder"
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "report for the sample folder data/"
```

**Test 2: Applies the record rules to line endings, spaces, comments and bad values** (hidden)

```bash
# Windows line endings, including a blank line that is only a carriage return.
mkdir -p crlf
printf 'date,employee,project,hours\r\n2026-09-01,Dee Shah,apollo,4\r\n\r\n2026-09-01,Dee Shah,Apollo,1.5\r\n' > crlf/dee.csv

actual=$(bash solution.sh crlf) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"
assert_eq "$actual" 'apollo 5.5
total 5.5
rejected 0' "a timesheet saved with Windows line endings"

# Lines to skip, and valid records written untidily.
mkdir -p tidy
{
  printf 'date,employee,project,hours\n'
  printf '\t# a comment after a tab\n'
  printf '   \n'
  printf '\t\n'
  printf ' date , employee , project , hours\n'
  printf '2026-09-02,Eli Novak,zephyr,0.5\n'
  printf ' 2026-09-03 ,\tEli Novak , ZEPHYR ,\t10 \n'
  printf '2026-09-04,Eli Novak,Zephyr,08\n'
} > tidy/eli.csv

actual=$(bash solution.sh tidy) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"
assert_eq "$actual" 'zephyr 18.5
total 18.5
rejected 0' "blank lines, comments, headers, spaces and tabs around fields, and project case"

# One valid record among lines that break each rule.
mkdir -p broken
{
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,2\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,.5\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,7.25\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,-2\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,8h\n'
  printf '2026-9-05,Fay Lund,orion,1\n'
  printf '05/09/2026,Fay Lund,orion,1\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,,3\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,   ,3\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion\n'
  printf '2026-09-05,Fay Lund,orion,1,5\n'
  printf 'see me about the orion hours\n'
} > broken/fay.csv

actual=$(bash solution.sh broken) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"
assert_eq "$actual" 'orion 2.0
total 2.0
rejected 12' "records that break the date, project, hours or field-count rules are rejected"
```

**Test 3: Finds every timesheet in the tree and reads every line of it** (hidden)

```bash
# A tree like the shared folder: months, a name with a space, files without a
# final newline, a directory whose name ends in .csv, and files to ignore.
mkdir -p tree/2026/09 tree/2026/10 tree/archive.csv
printf 'date,employee,project,hours\n2026-09-07,Ana Ruiz,apollo,3' > 'tree/2026/09/ana week 37.csv'
printf 'date,employee,project,hours\n2026-09-07,Ben Okafor,borealis,2.5' > tree/2026/09/ben.csv
printf '2026-10-01,Cleo Park,apollo,1\n' > tree/2026/10/cleo.csv
printf '2026-10-02,Dee Shah,cygnus,4\n' > tree/top.csv
printf '2026-10-03,Eli Novak,borealis,1\n' > tree/archive.csv/inner.csv
printf '2026-10-02,Dee Shah,cygnus,100\n' > tree/notes.txt
printf '2026-10-02,Dee Shah,cygnus,100\n' > tree/top.csv.bak
printf '2026-10-02,Dee Shah,cygnus,100\n' > tree/2026/OLD.CSV

expected='apollo 4.0
cygnus 4.0
borealis 3.5
total 11.5
rejected 0'

actual=$(bash solution.sh tree) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "every .csv file in the tree is read, and only those"

actual=$(bash solution.sh tree/) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status when the folder ends in /"
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "the folder given with a trailing slash"

mkdir -p 'shared folder'
cp -R tree 'shared folder/september export'
actual=$(bash solution.sh 'shared folder') || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status for a folder with a space in its name"
assert_eq "$actual" "$expected" "a folder whose name contains spaces"
```

**Test 4: Orders and formats the report, and handles empty folders and bad arguments** (hidden)

```bash
# Ordering by hours as numbers, ties by name, and decimal formatting.
mkdir -p order
{
  printf '2026-09-08,Gus Ito,alpha,3\n'
  printf '2026-09-08,Gus Ito,beta,1.5\n'
  printf '2026-09-09,Gus Ito,beta,1.5\n'
  printf '2026-09-08,Gus Ito,gamma,9.5\n'
  printf '2026-09-08,Gus Ito,delta,10\n'
  printf '2026-09-08,Gus Ito,kappa,0.1\n'
  printf '2026-09-09,Gus Ito,kappa,0.1\n'
  printf '2026-09-10,Gus Ito,kappa,0.1\n'
  printf '2026-09-08,Gus Ito,omega,0\n'
} > order/gus.csv

actual=$(bash solution.sh order) || fail "solution.sh exited with a non-zero status"
assert_eq "$actual" 'delta 10.0
gamma 9.5
alpha 3.0
beta 3.0
kappa 0.3
omega 0.0
total 25.8
rejected 0' "projects ordered by hours as numbers, ties by name, one decimal place"

# Folders with nothing to report.
mkdir -p empty quiet
printf 'date,employee,project,hours\n# nothing this month\n\n' > quiet/none.csv
for folder in empty quiet; do
  actual=$(bash solution.sh "$folder") || fail "a folder with no valid records must still exit with status 0"
  assert_eq "$actual" 'total 0.0
rejected 0' "a folder with no valid records"
done

# Bad arguments.
printf 'not a folder\n' > plain.txt
for args in none plain.txt no-such-folder; do
  if [ "$args" = none ]; then
    out=$(bash solution.sh 2> err.txt)
  else
    out=$(bash solution.sh "$args" 2> err.txt)
  fi
  status=$?
  assert_eq "$status" "2" "exit status when the argument is '$args'"
  assert_eq "$out" "" "standard output when the argument is '$args'"
  assert_eq "$(cat err.txt)" "usage: solution.sh DIRECTORY" "message on standard error when the argument is '$args'"
done
```
